utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Good morning. Please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-9-T, the Prosecutor versus Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic, Miroslav Tadic, and Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Prosecution is continuing examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear well now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yesterday I was asking you some questions about your life in Bosanski Samac and people you knew, including the defendants. Before I leave that topic, I just want to get a very brief overview of the property that you held as at April of 1992. Did you own a house or an apartment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had an apartment; I had my shop; I had a kombi van, which I used for practicing my profession; I had another small vehicle; I had video games, and the video games parlour was in a prefabricated building which was in the neighbourhood of my house; I also had a little boat, about eight, nine, ten metres long, and I used that for vacationing on the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And presumably your house had furniture and the usual domestic appliances and so on.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly that's the way it was, within the scope of my possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did your wife possess jewellery?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was some. Whenever I had the opportunity, I'd buy her some gold, silver, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We'll return to the fate of this property at a later point. There's been evidence in this trial of the existence of a body called the 4th Detachment. Were you aware of that, of that body?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When did you first become aware of its existence?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately five or six months before the war operations started.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How did you become aware of its existence?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out through what my acquaintances told me. They were talking about it, that they were called up in order to get into that unit itself. Allegedly, its purpose was to defend the town if there were to be some kind of an attack on the town of Samac. So later, I was also asked to come and join that unit, but I refused.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you understand it to be attached to the JNA?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You say that you were asked to join and that you refused. How was the invitation to join extended to you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a conversation between myself and Mr. Fadil Topcagic. He was explaining to me what the purpose of that unit would be. During this conversation, I came to a conclusion, and I said that to him, that in a neighbouring country there was already a war, and that war was waged by the Yugoslav People's Army, and they attacked the people and they shelled Vukovar and the other towns that are in our vicinity. And I said to him that that was more or less what was in store for us on the part of that same JNA and I did not want to be part and parcel of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When did you have this conversation?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This conversation took place, I can't say for sure now, but a few months earlier. Say it was five, five and a half, six months, before the war operations started, although Mr. Topcagic and I talked about the Fazan hunting club. We went hunting on a Sunday. We -- and then the shelling of Vukovar would start at 7.00 in the morning on that Sunday, so this was like four and a half months earlier, and I said to him, "See, Fadil, what you'd like us to get into." And that's when Fadil and I ceased all contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you mean you could hear the shelling in the distance?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the neighbouring Croatia. And we also saw all the telecasts and we heard the news and I knew that all of this was being done by the Yugoslav People's Army, and this unit that they offered me to join was also under the auspices of the Yugoslav People's Army, so I refused flatly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us if many Muslims in the municipality of Bosanski Samac joined the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not many, but individual persons did. There were some, though, who saw very quickly that this was not what they had been told originally. During the preparations, I had the opportunity of talking to my acquaintances. Actually, I know a gentleman who, just 15 days before the war, returned his rifle to this same Fadil. Actually, he told me that he returned it to Fadil, and he said that he didn't want to take part in this. And he got his family together and they all went to Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you comment on the proportion of Muslims who were members of the JNA -- of the -- sorry, of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mostly ethnic Serbs, and there were some Muslims, perhaps 5 per cent. I don't think it was even 5 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you comment on the number of Croats who were recruited into the ranks of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, because of course I did not have any insight into their documents, I don't know. I didn't hear of a single one being there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In the months leading up to April of 1992, did the 4th Detachment patrol the town of Bosanski Samac and the surrounding areas?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first observation was -- well, I had the opportunity of seeing a lot of suspicious things going on, but then I thought it wasn't much. However, just a few days before the war, a rally was held in town, and just before that rally - this was, say, at 9.00 or 10.00 or 11.00, I couldn't say for sure now -- actually, before that, my friends told me that the army was around town, all around town, and I didn't mind going to see all of this myself. So the town was besieged while this rally for peace was being held in town. I think that you'll understand what I'm saying. This was a rally of all citizens of all ethnic groups. People were publicly expressing their views, like there would be a war, there would not be a war, this and that, that we should live together, et cetera. However, that is to say that the actions and preparations of the 4th Detachment were already underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think I'd like you to explain a little more clearly what this rally has to do with the 4th Detachment. Why do you raise that issue of the rally in relation to the patrolling and the activities of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry for having interrupted. This is how I saw things. Since they probably thought that most people were not in favour of war, at least not in my opinion, everybody had their own business, their own work, their own family, and everybody was concerned, and they thought that there would be a lot of people attending that rally and that they could surround the town unhindered.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did the 4th Detachment have a presence at this rally?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Had you seen them publicly, that is the 4th Detachment, prior to this rally? For example, by patrolling or carrying out activities in the municipality of Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I did not have much opportunity, and actually, I wasn't all that interested either. All of this was always within the JNA, the JNA. That is to say that whatever would be said, they would say, that they were the Yugoslav People's Army, of course this forward unit, but of course, I could not consider this to be a normal thing because I did my military service, and after doing my military service, I was in the Territorial Defence and no one ever allowed me to take a rifle home. And as soon as I saw anybody with a military weapon that they had got from the 4th Detachment, that meant that that was not legal. And I did see people with weapons. Some people were actually bragging to me in a way, saying, "We have everything and you don't want to join us." There were things to that effect. However, on that day of the rally itself, there wasn't anything very important going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You just referred to seeing people with weapons and people bragging to you. Are you saying that they were members of the 4th Detachment? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely, because a gentleman who is related to Mr. Topcagic actually showed me a rocket launcher, and he said something like, "What are you guys with these little rifles going to do against us who have rocket launchers, tanks, and this and that?" Even then, though, I thought there could not be a war. I did not take this seriously. But I saw this with my very own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who was the person who showed you the rocket launcher?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His name was Senad. Believe me, as for the last name, it escapes me now. If I had more time, perhaps I could remember. However, I can explain the relationship between Fadil and this young man.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just tell us: Was this man Senad a member of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. He's the one who said that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's all I need to know. Did the SDA have any patrols, as far as you're aware, operating in the town of Bosanski Samac in the period of time prior to 16th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether the SDA did, but I know that there was a group of people that called themselves self-organised citizens, who wanted to protect their families and their town from a possible attack. I know about these people, that they were engaged in patrols. They even asked me to join them, but I didn't have time for that kind of thing. So that's what I can say about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: These people who called themselves the self-organised citizens, were they of a particular ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Most of them were Croats and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What sort of activities did they engage in?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the entrances into town, day and night, things could be seen, and they would stand there hiding, at least a bit, so that if they would see military vehicles or tanks coming in, they could go back into town and tell the rest of the population that possibly an attack was underway.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You were familiar, I think, with a Territorial Defence system that existed in the former Yugoslavia, also known as the TO?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, because after I did my military service, that is to say, in March 1975, I automatically joined the Territorial Defence, because that was the system of the state as it existed then, which meant that every able-bodied man up to the age of 55 or 60, whatever, was a reserve military conscript, and I was one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In the months, months, leading up to April of 1992, was it operating and existing in Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. This was a certain period when the Yugoslav People's Army came, collected all documents from the members of the Territorial Defence. As for the weapons that were stored for the municipality of Samac in case there was an aggression against Yugoslavia, there would be the possibility of a rapid intervention. That's the way the system functioned. So the TO did not exist after that, and until --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I apologise. I cut you off. Please finish your sentence.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. This TO, this Territorial Defence, came into being once again, say, a week before these war activities started.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, that's what I want to ask you about, the revival or re-establishment of the TO. How did you know that it was reviving or being re-established?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard that from my friends, from my acquaintances in town. The situation was rather tense, so people were talking. For me, this was a piece of good news, because knowing the TO from before, I thought that all three ethnic groups would be represented there, and as a matter of fact, I was pleased. And then I went there and signed up again, because with our own signatures we would confirm that we were yet again members of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Let's take it in a bit more detail. Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I came to the TO premises themselves. That was in a certain part of town that was not far away from the municipality building and the police station. I came there, and there were quite a few people there, and at one moment I realised that there were some specific people there, and I was really pleased to see one Serb, a few Croats, et cetera, and I thought: This is the right thing. We're all together again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just bear with me for one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I do apologise. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. So then I had to wait there for about half an hour, because there were quite a few people around. And then I walked in. I walked into the premises, into this room where there was a man sitting there, and he said, "This is a state institution, a military institution. The very name Territorial Defence means that we are defending the territory that we live in," and of course he explained all these things to me, and I very, very gladly accepted this, to become a member of the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's try to get a fix on the time, if we can. About how long before the 16th of April, 1992 was this?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps four or five or even six days earlier, give or take a day or two. A lot of time has gone by, and it's very hard to remember exactly, with precision, a particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown F50 from Exhibit P14; photograph number F50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: From P14A?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, yes. I'd ask the usher to make sure there is nothing on the photograph that indicates what the topic is. Thank you. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just have a quick look at that photo, please. Is that -- what building is that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the Territorial Defence building, the headquarters of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where did you go to sign up? Yes, use that baton to indicate.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you please turn it a bit this way? Yeah. This is where the entrance was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that there were a number of people there. Where were those people gathered?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was somewhere around here, see here, see here, within these ten metres or so, right in front of the entrance. Or actually, this entrance, this hallway, was already full of these people who were waiting to sign up to join the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm trying to get an idea after the sort of numbers that were gathered at the time that you went to sign up. What sort of crowd was there, if indeed it was a crowd?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. In my estimate, there were 150 or 200 people, and then, if you take into account those who were inside, perhaps it was about 250 altogether, because it took me a half hour to get in in order to sign up, and to sign these papers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What was the ethnic background of the crowd, as far as you could tell?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, they were Muslims. There were a few Croats and perhaps one or two Serbs. I can't say for sure now, but that's the people I saw there then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you aware of who was the Commander-in-Chief of this re-established TO?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. I was told, but I cannot really say now, who held which particular post. It was Mr. Marko Bozanovic and Mr. Alija Fitozovic. One was the commander and the other one was chief of staff, and I really cannot say which one held which of these two posts, although these are very, very high positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. That's fine. But can you tell us how you ascertained, how you found out, that those two men were holding the top positions in the TO?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, yes. As we were signing these papers, we were shown a document where it said that this -- how should I put this? That this appointment of theirs was confirmed by the minister from Sarajevo, so all of this was certified, whatever, so we realised that this was not just like that, that this was a legal institution of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. In the next few days, did you have occasion to return to the TO?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. One day I was passing by, two or three days afterwards, and I saw a crowd of people there. I stopped my car because I knew all the people very well who were there, so I stopped too, and I asked what was going on, what was happening, and they explained to me briefly and said that there were some weapons, and that this -- these weapons had to be taken over, and somebody even asked me why I didn't want to, and I said I didn't want to have any weapons, possess any weapons. I had my own hunting weapon. I didn't tell them that, but I was one of the people that had to procure my own weapon illegally; a rifle, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: First of all, again, can you comment on the numbers of people who were gathered on this second occasion that you describe? Was it the same as before or less?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less. There were about 40, a maximum of 50 people. Some were satisfied; others were not. There wasn't enough weapons. There weren't enough weapons to go around, and then they would get to this list and there were little problems there, and they asked me what am I looking for when I have a weapon? And I said I had a hunting rifle and that that's not why I was there. I was curious to see what was going on, that was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do I understand from that last answer that weapons were being distributed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Whether they were taking them off somewhere or whether there was a training session going on in the yard of the TO, I couldn't say with certainty now, but I would not be surprised if they had been distributing weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What sort of weapons were being -- or rather, what sort of weapons could you see being handled in the TO on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was rather out-of-date already. I can't say with certainty, of course, but probably it was what had remained, what was no good, and what the people that came before didn't want to take off with them, or perhaps they had procured it in some other way, the TO perhaps itself. So I can't say either way, but it was in pretty poor shape, the weaponry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How long did you remain there on this occasion, this second occasion?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, if I can just seek a clarification from you on the hunting weapon, you said that you had to procure your weapon illegally. Were you not entitled to a hunting weapon, a licence for your rifle, since you'd been a member of this hunting club for a long while?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there was a misunderstanding. Perhaps I didn't make myself clear. No. I came by my hunting weapon legally, but unfortunately, I procured an army weapon illegally too. I had that too. And that was only to protect my family and my property, and everything else, and I'm very happy to be able to say that I never used it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: So you had two weapons; a hunting rifle and another rifle?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had two hunting rifles. One was for small game and the other for big game, the carbine type and the shotgun. And I procured an army rifle illegally.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was that a Kalashnikov?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How long before the 16th of April did you acquire that weapon?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 10 to 15 days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you comment on the general availability of that sort of military rifle - I'm not talking about hunting rifles; I'm talking about military rifles such as a Kalashnikov - in the period of time leading up to April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, availability? In view of the fact that it was war in neighbouring Croatia, you could come by them. Of course, you had to pay for them and this ranged from 1.000 Deutschemarks to 2.000, or between 400 to 2.000, depending on the period. Prices changed. I know I had to pay a thousand marks for my own one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you ever see people carrying such weapons in the months leading up to April of 1992, carrying them about in the street, that sort of thing? I'm not talking about soldiers, okay; I'm talking about private citizens.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have occasion to see. It was just prior to the war, the situation, and nobody hid anything. Nobody bothered to hide anything, those who got it legally from the 4th Detachment and those of us who were not in the 4th Detachment. Of course, as far as I was able, I didn't carry my rifle around; I kept it away, and that's how I was parted from it too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now just return to this second occasion that you were at the TO and in which some weaponry was distributed. The TO is just across the road from the SUP building.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: On this second occasion, did you see any police officers observing what was going on at the TO?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Savo Cancarevic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What ethnic background is he?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a Serb. I know him very well because for a time he lived with my sister -- actually, he was married to my sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you see him on this second occasion when you were at the TO?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were standing up on the windows and watching it all. And later on this was reflected on us, because later on, through the camps and all the interrogations, they always claimed that it was illegal, an illegal institution, that TO, so it reverberated. For me, it was legal because it was the institution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, but probably that was the information that came back to them from the people that were looking out of the windows so that later on they could take it out on us in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'd like to refer you to two documents now. Can the witness please be shown D16/1. It's been marked only for identification. It's headed "The Communications Section." May I just see the document before the usher hands it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think you have the B/C/S version in front of you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Have you ever heard -- I'll withdraw that question. Cast your eye down the list of names.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know all these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Are they Muslim?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Have you ever heard of any body or organ or group called a communications section?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, quite certainly no, never. I never heard or saw anything like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Are any of those people there, to your knowledge, members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The gentleman by number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Ibrahim Kabaklic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ibrahim Kabaklic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where is he now?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And even -- that is to say, I think he's in Australia or Canada now, but up to the war, or in the war, he was in the army of Republika Srpska, in the 4th Detachment, at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What about number -- what about Alija Drljacic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. It's leading, obviously.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll withdraw --

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: This is a leading way of examination. The witness should -- the first question was -- after reviewing the names, the witness can say, to the best of his knowledge, whom does he have information about the 4th Detachment membership.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You've commented on one person that you know to be a member of the 4th Detachment. Can you see any other people there who were, to your knowledge, also members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I didn't pay attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who else?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or if the Court allows me to, let me just say that this is the second time in my life that I'm in a court of law, so I'm a little nervous. First of all was in Bijeljina, in the military court. So I haven't got much experience in matters of this kind. So I should like to say thank you to the gentleman, but please try and understand. Yes, Kemal Dzakic, the man who returned his rifle 15 days before the war and said he did not wish to take part with them in all that, and he left for Germany. And Mr. Alija Drljacic is an elderly man who died several months ago. He was about 65 years old. He was an old man and not a conscript. I don't know about this list, but I can say this -- present these facts on the basis of this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to clarify some things from your last answer. You say Kemal Dzakic returned his rifle 15 days before the war and didn't want to take part in all of that. Returned his rifle to whom? We have to be precise.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I didn't see that case, but that's what he told me, word by word. He said, "I returned the rifle to Fadil and Simo and told them that I do not wish to take part in that." And one or two days later, he collected up his family and left for Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And I don't want to be pedantic, but you haven't actually said: Was he actually a member of the 4th Detachment up until the time that he handed back his rifle?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was. He was armed by them, according to what he had said some two months previously, which means that he already possessed the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you also commented on a gentleman named Alija Drljacic. Now, was he actually a member of the 4th Detachment or not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he wasn't a member of the 4th Detachment, but he was an elderly man, and according to all military structures, he wouldn't be eligible for a list of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is he still alive, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He died, unfortunately, this year.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How old was he back in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, he was about 64 or 65, perhaps a year or two more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with that document. Can the witness now be shown D17/1. I believe this document has also been marked for identification. And it should be headed "Hunters' Section."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, again, cast your eye down the list of names, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've had a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know if any of the men listed there were members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who? Which one? Which one or ones were members?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me just see. The first is number 6, Mr. Dzevad Seljakovic who stayed there. I don't know whether he stayed until the end of the war, but I know that he's abroad somewhere now. Well, that man, number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. Did he have brothers?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were they in the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had four brothers. With the exception of one, all of them were in the 4th Detachment. Seljakovic, Fikret, and the other one's name I can't quite remember now. I can't remember his name now, but there was Dzevad, there was Fikret, and I think that third one's name was -- I can't remember. But the Seljakovic brothers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, in your evidence you've commented on the existence of this body called Fazan, or Pheasant, which was the hunting club. Were any of the men listed in D17/1 members of Fazan?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Here is the man, just as he is here in this hunters' section, commander Hasan Mesanovic was for a long time president and secretary of the society, and Mr. Pasaga, he was too. Mehmed, Dzevad Jusufovic, Kemal Bajraktarevic, a hunter, yes. In fact, they were all hunters, not to go through the whole list, they were all hunters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What about Avdo Drljacic? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts He's the only one I'm not quite sure of. He was doing his sort of training. He wasn't a full-fledged hunter, but he went hunting with us. I can't say for sure whether he had actually become a hunter, passed his sort of test, or whether he was to become a full-fledged hunter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I just want to ask you very briefly about some of the personal details of these men. Can you tell us how old number 5, Enes Drljacic, was in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less, that would be a bit difficult. But Mehmedalija Tihic was 50 years old. The others were younger. He was a notorious alcoholic. Sevko was a retired policeman. Enes Drljacic was about 60, as I've already said. Just a moment, please. There is a mistake here. Mehmedalija Tihic was not a notorious alcoholic. That's somebody else. I was thinking of Tiric, nicknamed Mesa. He was the man I was thinking of. And I think all the people who knew him -- those of them here who knew him knew that he was an alcoholic. Mustafa Salkic was about 60. The other, Pasaga, was a little younger. So they were -- some of them were between 60 and 65, along with the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I've dealt with those documents. I want to ask you now about events on the night of the 16th of April, 1992. There has been evidence in the case that that was the night on which an attack occurred -- sorry, hostilities commenced in Bosanski Samac. Where were you on the night of the 16th and 17th of April?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depending on the period you have in mind, if you're thinking about the actual time before the attack, I was sleeping at my own home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's where I want to pick things up from, and I want to start hearing your account of events from that point onwards. You said you were at home. Were you awoken?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. [redacted] [redacted]. And across the road not far from the MUP, the TO and the municipality building, a man stepped out in front of his car wearing a camouflage uniform. He was armed. He had black paint on his face. And this gave rise to the suspicion that the attack on town had begun. But as this was in the same direction, he went straight on to my house, he woke me up and said, "It seems that the attack has started." I dressed quickly, and then took up that rifle of mine, the one that I had procured illegally, and we went off.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us how you dressed? What you were wearing, I should say.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I had hunting trousers on and a jumper of some kind, or a T-shirt or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What colour were the hunting trousers?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were green hunting trousers, the standard type of wear that hunters wear, all green.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where did you [redacted] go?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went off in that direction, in the direction that he had seen the people, and he sort of thought intuitively -- and we of course knew that part of town, we knew all the streets, and we knew that there was an intersection, a crossroads, and that they could reach the street in front of the MUP via the yards. So we turned off one street earlier, and at the time we were there, we were conscious of the fact that they had covered the whole area, so we didn't come out onto that street directly. We -- but we got there, and we got out of the car. And at that particular moment, a police car came up on the left-hand side, and in it we recognised Mr. Namik Suljic, and we managed to divert him to the left. We made sign language to tell him that something bad was going on. And at the point when he turned left, there was shelling, and a shell hit the balcony of the MUP building. The shooting started. And that's how it all began. And the events followed on after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who is Namik Suljic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Namik Suljic was the commander of the reserve police force, and that night he was actually on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You say that the MUP was struck by fire. Where -- what was the direction of --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It hit the balcony. Of course, they weren't large shells. MUP was not set fire to. It just hit the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, perhaps I misled you. What I meant was that it was struck by shells or bullets. I wasn't suggesting that it was put on fire. But what I was interested in was the direction from which the fire was being -- was coming towards the MUP, the firing, I should say.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's difficult for me to demonstrate this without anything. Perhaps if I had a photograph, then it would be much easier and I could explain it quite easily, if I had something to work with.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I don't want to dwell on this. I don't want to dwell on this for too long. I just want to know the general direction from which the firing was occurring.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'll try. I'll try to describe this to you. The shell came from round about the area -- actually, opposite is the TO building, where there was a spare parts shop, car shop there, so it would be from the edge of the TO building or this shop selling spare parts for cars, in the direction of the balcony. And then there was shooting from rifles, there were screams, people shouting, "Come out and surrender." We were about 60 metres away, so we could hear all this fairly well. And it was a bit dangerous, so we decided to withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went towards the centre of town again, because in the evening we saw that Namik managed to return by car along that street that runs along the Sava River. We went the other way and then we met up with Mr. Namik by the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What did you do at the hotel?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was not at the hotel, or rather, in the hotel; it was by the hotel. We did not enter the hotel. He told us that he had already informed his patrols, these police patrols like, because they were probably already being called to go back. But Namik told them, through radio communications, that they should not return to the police station because they would be taken prisoner there. And then he said that he had this great worry that he did not know what was going on with the people at the bridge, because he also had the bridge under his control. So then we just talked a little bit, very fast. We were all lost because, actually, war had already started.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Which bridge did you understand him to be referring to?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant the bridge on the Sava River because, just before the war, that bridge had been mined and then the police was guarding the bridge. These people from the police were at the bridge at that given moment. And later on, it turned out that Namik had been right, because these people were taken prisoner either by the 4th Detachment or the JNA or whoever. I cannot confirm that. At any rate, they were taken prisoner, and as I proceed to testify, you will probably hear more about these people too, these people who were taken prisoner by the bridge at the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. So Mr. Namik expressed his concerns. You were gathered at the -- near the hotel. What was your next move?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this had already been going on for 10, 15, perhaps even 20 minutes. Since there was no organisation there -- I mean, how shall I put this? There was no military command that would tell us, "Come here," "Be there," "Take your weapons," the way things were in the previous system, when I knew exactly where the assembly point was and at every time of day or night I knew where I shall come if I were called up. However, that did not exist now. We were not organised. People were getting out of buildings into the street. Everybody was afraid. Everybody was wondering what was going on. Some people were asking me, and I was asking other people, "Do you know what happened? Do you know what's going on?" So people were panic-stricken as well. Then we decided to move towards the river, towards the bridge, because we thought that probably the army was not there yet. However, when we got there, the army had already arrived. And now, at that particular moment, it reminded me of what had happened a few days earlier. That had actually been like a dress rehearsal for what was supposed to happen on that day, that is to say, having the town of Bosanski Samac besieged by the 4th Detachment. Because the town was practically surrounded, besieged. You could not get out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: First of all, which bridge are you referring to? You say that you decided to move towards the bridge. Which bridge?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The bridge on the Bosna River. You crossed that bridge in order to get to the village of Prud, to Dubica, and these other places. This is a small bridge on the Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And you commented that events reminded you of what had happened a few days earlier, and you referred to a dress rehearsal. What exactly did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I said during the introduction, when this rally took place in town, Samac had already been surrounded, besieged. I think I already explained that. The 4th Detachment was all around and everybody knew what they were supposed to do. The town was surrounded, besieged. Nobody could get out of it. I, for one, experienced that. I tried to cross the bridge, and then, on the left-hand side of the bridge, as I was walking across it, they started firing against me from bunkers. They were shooting at me. Fortunately, this bridge had a concrete fence, so to speak, and you can imagine me, weighing 120 kilogrammes, crawling in order not to be hit. So they were shooting. All the civilians who went towards that bridge and onto that bridge were being shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You say that civilians were going towards that bridge. Can you comment on the numbers of civilians?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what, I think I would have to describe this event itself in greater detail. I managed to cross the bridge, but until then, nobody had crossed it. As I crossed the bridge - I heard that Mr. Kukrika, a Serb, I hear that he's deceased - they did not shoot at us, we did not shoot at them. We told them to move away, and that's what they did. So if they had stayed there and if they were shooting, no civilians would stand a chance of crossing the bridge. Later on, it turned out that we were right that we drove them out of those bunkers on the left-hand side. Three hundred or three hundred fifty men, women, and children managed to get out of town and thereby not experience what everybody else had gone through, later, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I just want to clarify a couple of matters. Why did you cross the bridge to Prud in the first place? Why did you try and do that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean? Are you referring to me only or all the people who were there?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: As I understand your evidence, you went to the bridge that goes to Prud and that you crossed the bridge alone. During that time, you were fired at. Now, what was your reason? Why did you want to cross the bridge at that time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, that was the only way out to freedom. A gentleman managed to pass with me. Nedim Alajbegovic was his name, I think. The two of us managed to cross the bridge and get to the village of Prud, and over there we found some people who were already there, because shooting had already started in town and they already heard that war had broken out in Samac. And they asked me what was going on, and then I explained the situation to them and I said what the situation was. And I said that if we did not get those people out of those bunkers by the bridge, nobody would manage to get out of town, because whoever would get to the bridge, they would shoot at them, just as they fired at me and at Mr. Nedim. And they said that they could help us. They even gave me this little walkie-talkie thing - what's it called? - a Motorola, so that we'd have some kind of communications device. And then we were supposed to go back and to try to organise ourselves so that these people could be driven out of there so that it would be possible for civilians to get out. Even though I had a rifle, I never considered myself to be a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you carrying the weapon at that time?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment, no. No, because as I was crawling across the bridge, I left it way behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who were you meant to communicate with using the Motorola walkie-talkie?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I communicated with people in Prud. People organised themselves within the local commune because they probably already saw what was going on. In Croatia, they were a bit more organised than we were, so they already had this kind of small communications centre of their own, whatever. I did not have much experience with that kind of thing. And that proved itself by the fact that the enemy side managed to listen in on all my conversations, like that we should not go anywhere, that the Chetniks would come and slaughter us, you know, things like that. It was pretty awful.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you return to Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I managed to. I managed to. The same way I left. I went back into Bosanski Samac crawling too, because that's where my family was, my wife and children, and everything I had actually was there. So I went back. I simply could not just leave them there, and I couldn't just remain sitting out there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: On this second trip back across to Bosanski Samac, was the -- were the machine-gun emplacements firing on you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, from three directions. There was gunfire coming on that bridge. Just as they did not let people get out, they didn't let people get back. However, I managed to get back, and also this gentleman went back with me, Mr. Nedim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you do anything about the machine-gun emplacements firing on the bridge? Or indeed, did anyone else do anything about them?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were some more people there by now. Some were armed; others were not; others had this; others had that. So how should I put this? There was some kind of organisation already set up, and I had already come there when they had reached a decision that we should try to get rid of these three machine-gun emplacements so that it would be possible to get across the bridge. People who were from the 4th Detachment, who were on the embankment, they agreed to withdraw completely. Nobody shot at anyone over there. However, the people from the machine-gun emplacements continued to shoot. So we didn't really dare go that way. So we withdrew, and of course, some of the people who knew a bit more about things like that did manage to get rid of this machine-gun fire. They withdrew. That's for sure. So that was already a big, a big advantage for us, that women and children and men, regardless of age, managed to get out of the besieged town of Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You say there were some kind of organisation already set up. What was this organisation already set up that you refer to?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what I mean by that is when there are five, ten, 15, 20, 50 of us there, that we managed to do something. Nothing much, but we managed to self-organise this thing. We'd say, "Okay, let's go out and do this, let's do that." That's what I meant. I did not mean an organisation. All of us were distressed. None of us had any experience of war, we did not have any preparations for war, whereas others had already carried that out for months before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did civilians eventually start to use the bridge to cross over to Prud?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This lasted until just before the evening, when APCs and tanks got into town. They crossed the bridge again. They went back to their old positions. And from then onwards, nobody could get out. Later on, people started trying to escape through mine fields in order to reach the Sava River, the Bosna River. Many tried to swim even in the winter period, and we know that they drowned. Even on Christmas, on the 25th of December, 1992, when people got call-up papers, this man did not want to take a rifle and he tried to swim across the river, and then during the winter, he tried to swim across, and this is 300, 400 metres. One of them, unfortunately, drowned, the other one managed to get to the other side. And as far as mobilisation is concerned, they said that people had to take rifles of the Republika Srpska. I don't know whether it was called the Republika Srpska at that time. They said that there was no other option but to swim through the murky waters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm really interested, though, in the events of the night of the 16th and 17th at this stage. Let's stick with that. You've said that civilians managed to get across until the evening. Do I understand, then, that they were crossing the bridge all day, that is, all day of the 17th?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, people were crossing the bridge, but a lot of people from town, first of all, did not even know about this, and secondly, they didn't dare go, because there was already panic throughout town. Looting had already started. People were taken into custody. There was intimidation. Many didn't know about this, and also they simply did not have the courage to go to that bridge where they could somehow get out to freedom. At 5.00, 4.30 or 5.30 in the evening, this had already become sealed off. Even if they wanted to, they could not get out after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you actually see civilians crossing the bridge to Prud?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What ethnic background were they?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, most of them were Muslims and Croats, except for one who I personally managed to see, and he was a Serb. This was an elderly man, Mr. Zivko Stajic. For many years, he was a member of the Fazan hunting club and he gave his hunting rifle to a young man and he said, "Take it. Struggle against them, fight against them, if you can, because I also fought against people like that in the Second World War." So he is one of the people who crossed the bridge over there as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: At the time that you saw people, civilians, crossing the bridge, can you tell the Court what sort of numbers that you actually observed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I managed to see, these were smaller groups of civilians, because people were afraid of going in bigger groups because then there could be shooting again. So there were three, four or five persons per group, and they were crossing the bridge, but they were bent forward because they were afraid a bullet could come from somewhere. I managed to see some 50 odd people, 70, whatever. I mean, it never occurred to me that I should start counting them or whatever. But I know, according to some information, that about 350 to 400 people managed to get out, thanks to the fact that this bridge was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What are your sources of information on the 350 to 400 people? How do you know that? Who told you that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I got that information - well, perhaps, it was even quite accurate - when I was exchanged. So people talked and said that this family got out, that family got out, and that this figure was around 400 persons altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown photographs 34 and 35, F34 and F35 from P14A, please. And if we could deal with number 34 first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you recognise that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the remains of the bridge that was once there; the bridge on the Bosna River, since there are two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What country is the far bank in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's also Bosnia-Herzegovina, but that's the village of Prud on the other side. I'm talking about the bridge on the Bosna River, because I know that area very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And the bridge depicted in this photo is the same bridge in which civilians were crossing?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pantelic?

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: I ask my dear friend to be more precise, because with this formulation, it seems that this -- that was a condition of the bridge in April 1992, and then the civilians were forced to go over this kind of bridge. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'll clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Perhaps you heard Mr. Pantelic's concern. Can you tell us if that's what the bridge looked like on the night that the civilians were crossing, or was it intact?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I heard that the gentleman's name is Mr. Pantelic, so I will explain it to him, but if he listened carefully, I said very precisely that these are the remains of the bridge. That was not the bridge the people were crossing. You can see that you cannot cross this bridge. These are the remains of the bridge. The bridge was all right then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Could you have a look at the next photograph, 35. What does that depict?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when you go from Prud, you enter Samac from the bridge, and you see the town of Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So this is, in effect, the view from bridge to Prud, looking back towards Samac? Have you had the question translated? I'll repeat my question. Photograph number F35, does that depict the view from the bridge to Prud back towards Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, if you -- I'll withdraw that question. You've commented on machine-gun fire being directed towards the bridge to Prud. Can you use the baton to indicate, as best you can, where the machine-gun emplacements were that were firing on the bridge?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, got back here and then it's behind this house that you see here. There is a clearing. There is a clearing behind it. And then there is about 300 or 350 metres to the Bosna River, to near the embankment, and that's where the machine-gun emplacements had a good overview of this road, of this corner and the bridge itself on the Bosna river. That is to say that, from these machine-gun emplacements, they had a total view of this entire area, the bridge and practically the entire bridge. Unfortunately, you can't really see all of this on this picture, but I could explain all of this to you, exactly where things are.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So those civilians who you've referred to crossing the bridge would have had to go down this road, or rather, up this road, towards the bridge, and cross over?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there's one more thing I'd like to say. It was not the way people went because of the safety concerns. Nobody really had the courage to move this way, this way. Can you see me? But it was this way. And also, here there is this small bridge, see? So then you'd get off there and then walk along the embankment and then underneath it. And then just here, where the bridge was, where the bridge was over here, then people would hastily get onto the bridge and cross it. There were some people who took their cars and got out that way. They are the only ones who had to pass through here directly. So for our own safety, we went this way. Because this road, this road, is higher than the ground, say four metres higher, so there was a kind of natural shelter that they had.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm done with that photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Your family was still in the town when you crossed over back into Bosanski Samac?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Our clock is 11.00, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- we'll have our break and resume our proceedings at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. di Fazio. You are continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Just before I do continue, we have at this moment, just prior to Your Honours entering the Chamber, been provided with a number of documents by Mr. Zecevic, being statements of this witness that were taken in 1992. It wasn't given to us because I understand Mr. Zecevic was having translation problems, and indeed I understand the documents still haven't been translated. Whatever the reason, the fact is that we've now been given these statements, and they're not statements or material that was within the possession of the Office of the Prosecutor and that have come from our archives, so to speak, not material that we have. I therefore find myself in a position of being given this material, not knowing what the witness says about the material, and so on; the usual disadvantages that would arise from such a situation. I propose, therefore, with the Chamber's approval, if it's acceptable to the Chamber, that we do what we did on a previous occasion, namely, instruct the investigating officer in this case to go and speak to the witness at some stage with the documents, as soon as we've got a rough translation, at least, and answer a few basic queries about the documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So would that -- how many statements have you been given?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: We've been given two statements and another document. The other document doesn't concern me so much, but it's the two statements that I do want to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. How many pages are they? Because -- although that doesn't really matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: About four pages. There's one, and two on the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And they're from -- what are their dates? Or you can't read the Serbo-Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I can't read them, but I think one is 26th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Maybe Mr. Zecevic can help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, by all means, Your Honour. Actually, I notified, ten days in advance, the Prosecutor's office of the existence of these statements, just before Mr. Hasan Bicic was cross-examined, because I received them at that time, and I notified the Prosecutor that I have all these statements. And immediately upon receiving these statements, because of the urgency, I have translated the Hasan Bicic statement, and the rest of the statements were given to the Registry for the official translation. I was told by the Registry that by last Friday we will have these translations. Not until this moment. So I gave to the Prosecutor these documents in B/C/S. I know it creates a problem for them, but I mean, there isn't any -- much more that I can do. We can do an unofficial translation again, if that helps them, but that is the situation. I'm sorry, but it's beyond me, so to speak. Actually, these are the statements. One of the statements was taken in Brcko but the JNA barracks in Brcko, like the previous two, and one is a statement from the police station in Bosanski Samac, as well as like previous two. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. So the Prosecution is asking for leave of the Chamber to have the witness -- the investigator get instructions on those statements from the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's right. Essentially, proof the witness on what he says about the documents, and any other information that we might need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: During lunch break or --?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, I would hope to -- definitely before the close of his examination-in-chief, and I would hope at the lunch break, but I don't know what the investigator is doing. I found out about it just now, so I can't say precisely when or what arrangements will be made, except to say that I -- the broad outline of my proposal is give them to the Prosecutor and ask him to go and speak to the witness when the witness is free, presumably during the lunch break or at the close of today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The Trial Chamber would appreciate that. I'm sure you can send instructions through one of your colleagues to the investigator concerned or to somebody who can read Serbo-Croat, so that you do it during lunch hour, because we are trying as much as possible to avoid detaining witnesses unduly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Of course, and I appreciate the Chamber's concerns and I'll attend to that, make sure it's done quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We don't have any objection, of course, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I assumed you wouldn't because it's a problem beyond your control. In order to avoid this sort of problem - because our translation units or whatever they are called, the people who have to deal with Serbo-Croat, English or French, are quite overloaded - so I think it's prudent for Defence counsel, if they have any documents which are in Serbo-Croat, even without them being translated, to give copies to the Prosecution as quickly as possible, explaining, of course, that you are training to push through translation, but if they can get translation, because maybe they have their own services, then we will have no problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We will do that, Your Honours, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, just before you start, if you would be good enough to refer the witness to Exhibit P9, the map, and just get him to identify the bridge over the Bosna River.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And I think also the road that leads from the village to the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, that can be done. Indeed, I have a clean copy here which can probably be used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. It's a clean copy of the same?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's a clean copy. I'm just wondering if I should use P9. Could I perhaps have a look at P9?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: What's the correct number of the exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The exhibit, that one, is P9D.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I think it might be preferable to use --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: A clean copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, yes. I think it would be preferable to use a clean copy, so I hand up P9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So we can have the main number and then the next letter to it. Can we just have the number for the new copy?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: New copy will be numbered P9E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Salkic, can you please indicate on that, with the blue marking pen, the bridge that leads to Prud, and also the roadway that you saw in photograph number 35, the roadway leading from the Prud bridge back to Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is the pen not working?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but not very well. That's Prud.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Might I just see the exhibit? Fine. Thank you. Yes, okay. Then, thank you very much. And perhaps that can be returned now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Can we just have -- how has he marked them, one or two?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No. I was just about to say that, if Your Honour pleases, for the purposes of the transcript, the witness has marked the map in blue marking pen. It's clearly visible to the naked eye. It's not so visible on the ELMO device. But you'll be able to see it very clearly on the actual exhibit itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: How many places has he marked?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: He's marked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: One or two?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: One -- he's marked one particular stretch of terrain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Okay. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Leading from the town of Bosanski Samac to Prud.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Perhaps if you use another pen --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I put an arrow from the village of Prud towards the entrance of Samac, so not from Samac. But this marker pen is a little thick, but as far as I understood the question, I was supposed to show the road from the village of Prud to Samac, and that's what the arrow shows. That's the direction of the arrow that I drew in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you use another pen, please? Thank you. Indeed, I think it's red. Can you mark the road that we could see from the bridge back to Bosanski Samac, from the bridge leading in towards Bosanski Samac. Can you mark that in red.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Good. Thank you. Is that sufficient for the Chamber's purposes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Sorry, just is that the road in P35?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I believe it is, if Your Honour pleases, but perhaps I'll just ask the witness to have a look at P35 -- sorry, F35 of Exhibit P14A. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, you've seen this photograph before, Mr. Salkic. Is that the roadway that you have depicted in red on the map?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to return to the events of the 17th of April. Your family was still in Bosanski Samac at the time that you came back in via the bridge?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What did you do after you re-entered Bosanski Samac via the bridge?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first saw those people there, as I already said, people beginning to gather. There were people on the streets. Some were walking around, coming, coming out. Others were looking out of the window. It was wartime. Actually, the war started in Bosanski Samac between the 16th and 17th, that evening, that night, so in fact, it was a state of war. Samac was occupied. What can I say? Occupied by that army, the army that was in Bosanski Samac at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just very briefly, there appears to be a mistake in the translation. I asked you earlier a question whether the roadway that you can see in photograph F35 was the portion of the map that you marked in red. You answered but no translation appears in the transcript. What is your position? Is that -- the portion in red on the map the same road that can be seen in F35?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the entrance. When you cross the bridge, you enter the town of Samac and that is that particular road.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. Now let's get back to the events in Bosanski Samac. This confused state existed in the town. Did you try to get back to your family?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you succeed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I even -- at one point, I was with them. But I thought that the time was not right yet, and that the individuals -- that perhaps the individuals were right and that we could cross the river too, because it was the only way of getting to freedom. And when I say this, I mean that I was not allowed to move around freely. The telephones had been cut. There was shooting somewhere in the distance. It was just a question of time when this whole thing would come to the centre of town, where I was. But unfortunately, some time went by, and on the eve of the time that I made my decision to leave, at the approach to the bridge, people sent me back. That was about half past 4.00, 5.00, towards evening. They told me not to go there because the bridge had been taken over. I said, "How do you mean, taken over?" And they said, "The people from the 4th Detachment are there and nobody can leave." So from that time on, 4.00 or 5.00, Samac was totally blocked, because none of the Croats or Muslims were able to leave after that time, unless they found some other way of doing that, whether they bribed someone or perhaps a Serb friend had succeeded in taking someone out of town. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not then. Not yet. My arrest was to come later on, on the 18th. Because of some people who I say may, may, have problems - it's not sure that they would - but they were Serbs who helped me to spend that particular night hidden in their homes, and I left in the morning. Do you want me to start telling you about that? Do you want me to recount what happened, the sequence of events that followed, or is it enough for me to tell you that I was with my family, in answer to your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were not arrested on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What date were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was arrested -- it was Saturday, the 18th, the morning of Saturday, the 18th. And I think that's what it says in my statement, that I was arrested on the 18th.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where did you spend the night?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing is if --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where did you spend the night of the 17th?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just explained that. I don't want to mention names unless the Trial Chamber absolutely insists, because, as I say, maybe, and I stress maybe, some of these people might -- there might be repercussions on these people. So if I don't absolutely have to give their names, then I would rather not, because they were Serbs who helped me spend the night safely at their place, because searches had already begun in town, arrests and that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was your family with you when you were sheltering with these Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I left them at my mother-in-law's. She was a Serb, so that I thought they would be sufficiently safe and secure staying with her.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When you were sheltering at the home of these Serbs who assisted you, were you armed? Did you have your rifle with you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. No. Those people were very much afraid, because they were afraid of what would happen to them if some of the other Serbs would turn up and find me there. They probably wouldn't have had a good time of it. So I should like to say that I'm grateful to them for at least saving me the hardships for one night that I was later to experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: During that period of time that you were at the home of these people, were you able to see soldiers or military people in the streets?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The town was flooded with soldiers. I did not leave that night, because -- but these friends of mine said that it was terrible, that there was general looting, that they were just looking to see what they could loot and plunder. So it was terrible not so much because of the war but because of all this looting going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you see any members of the 4th Detachment?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I could see from the window, because the person that I stayed with drew the curtains so that nobody could see from outside who was inside, and even if they came to his door, they knew that he was a Serb, which meant that they wouldn't enter his house and search the place, so that I more or less felt safe.
