And then from time to time I would hear the noise they were making and the swearing of the soldiers, but I can guarantee that none of the Croats or Muslims dared go out into the street that night.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were arrested on the 18th. Where were you arrested?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was arrested in front of my own house. I took advantage of the occasion to go to my wife's, to see my wife and children, and I said that I would probably leave home, take some documents with me and, at great risk, that I would try to reach the river Sava, although it was actually snowing that morning and the water was very high, 700, 800 metres. But I said I'd risk that. I would try to swim for it, to swim to freedom, and if I survived, well and good; if not, maybe somebody would shoot me before that. But I didn't succeed in carrying out what I intended to do. I went home to get my documents, and at that moment, some armed people turned up in front of my house and they told me to get ready. Well, actually, no, not to get ready; just to go out, not to take any weapons, to put my hands up, and if I failed to do so, they said they would shell my house, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can I ask you, how old were your children at that stage?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My daughter was 3 1/2 at the time, two months more, that is to say, 3 years and 8 months - her birthday was the 16th of February, and this coincides - whereas my son was 11 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You left them with their mother?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with their mother, at my mother-in-law's house. And I said that she was a Serb and that that is why I thought they would be safe there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The people who arrested you, did you recognise any of them?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who were they?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Cviko or Cvikan Tesic, Savo Tesic, Fadil Topcagic and several others. I can't remember their names now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was there any -- did they have any vehicles with them?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was a police car. Well, we'll take this in order. Yes, there was a police car. They put me in it and drove me off to the MUP, or SUP, as it was previously known.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we do that, though, I want to ask you: Did Fadil Topcagic speak to you at the time that you were arrested outside your house?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At one point, he said, "Well, that's what happens when you did not know to choose the right side." Perhaps I understood him, perhaps I didn't, but now things have become crystal clear to me what he meant when he said that: the real side, the proper side or right side.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How was he and the others who were with him dressed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were wearing camouflage uniforms. Some of them had the uniforms that were worn by the JNA. They all had bands here. I don't remember the colour, but I think they were white. They all had these white shoulder bands.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I think the transcript should show that the witness indicated the top of his left arm, at the top, near the shoulder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What about Fadil Topcagic? Did he have the white armband?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You said you were put in a car and taken to the MUP. Who accompanied you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two soldiers. One of them was a lieutenant by rank. I didn't notice the rank of the other one. I'm not sure about the second one. But they were wearing camouflage uniforms and also had that insignia, or they had the shoulder pads, epaulettes, that were worn by the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What scene greeted you at the MUP?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat that question here? I didn't understand the first word.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. What sort of things did you see when you first arrived at the SUP or MUP?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ah, yes. I would like to mention at this point that during my arrest and transport, there was no beating, but those two soldiers, the lieutenant and the other one, their conduct was exceptionally proper. They were very proper and they brought me to the MUP building and we got out. When I went through the main entrance of the MUP, there they started beating me. That's when it all started. But -- well, it was terrible, but later on, I realised that things could get much worse and that they were very mild towards me at that point. They took me inside. The corridor was on the left, and the room was on the right. It was the duty office of the officer on duty. They took me in there. And that's where I met two men. One of them was Stevan Todorovic and the other one I was later to learn was Crni, nicknamed Crni - that was his nickname - and another policeman who was on duty there and worked with the communication lines. At that particular moment -- do you want me to go on? Do you want me to describe that moment at which I entered the building? He began beating me -- Stiv began beating me, and this other man, this gentleman - I say "gentleman," but actually he was a dark man and I didn't know who he was at that time - he told him not to beat me because he said I would -- they would need me afterwards, and he told them to put me into a cell. So I was taken out of that office into the corridor, and on the right-hand side, there were two cells. And when I got there, I found quite a number of people already there before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How many people?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot remember all the details but I can remember some people. I can even remember certain names, quite a few names. I think there were about 12, 10, 13 of us, whatever. There were two cells. But given all that fear and everything else, I wouldn't be certain of the number, but it was around ten to 15 persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they were Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Any of them apparently military types or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. All of them wore civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: At the time that Crni said -- at the time that Crni said they would need you afterwards, did you have any idea what he meant at that time when he said that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, but soon I found out, because this is what happened: These same two soldiers who brought me, who drove me to the SUP, this lieutenant and the other man, they put me in a police vehicle. One of them sat behind me, the lieutenant, and he dictated a certain text to me, and that was roughly --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you? May I just interrupt you here? Before you were taken out of the cell and taken into the police vehicle, did you see any of the defendants?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Could you explain this to me? Defendant or Defence counsel? What does this word "defendant" mean? Perhaps I didn't quite understand it. Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just so that you understand me, when I speak of the defendants, I'm referring to the gentlemen you identified yesterday; Simo Zaric, Miroslav Tadic, Blagoje Simic, Milan Simic. That's what I mean by "defendant." My question is: Before you were taken out of the MUP and placed in the police car, did you see any of those gentlemen?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I saw Mr. Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him -- well, I saw him there. He was in front of the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What was he --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the guard opened the cell -- well, I was about to find out what the purpose was. The guard opened the door and he said, "Let my guys get out." We all practically started out from the door, because we were all from the same town. However, unfortunately, only four men got out, and all the rest of us remained locked inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who were the four who got out?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try to remember. Sometimes I'll mention a nickname; sometimes I'll mention a name and surname. But anyway, it was Mr. Mujaga, I think his last name is Omeranovic. The other one was Seljakovic. I think -- well, his nickname is Mrki. I can't remember his first name. And then there was Mr. Kapetanovic, Muharem, nicknamed Sora. And the fourth one, I think, was Fikret Avdic Asim. And we knew earlier on that they were in the 4th Detachment, and then it became clear to us who his guys were, and we were not his and that's why we were left there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did he leave with them?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. The cell door closed and there were bars on it. I can't go into all the details. They left. We stayed behind. And then it all started, the beatings, this and that and the other thing. And then soon after that, there was another thing that happened. I was picked up by two men. I started telling you about this. The one with Crni. And actually, Crni said that they should take me and that I should take care of this thing, and then I realised why Crni did not realise -- did not let me be beaten by Stiv Todorovic nicknamed Monstrum. I realised that they needed me for something but I did not know what for. I realised that only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now I'd like you to tell us about this episode.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So they took me out of the cell, they took me out of the police station, they put me in a Golf, a police vehicle, a Golf, a police Golf, and then this lieutenant -- he did have a rank, that's what mattered; the other one did not. The other one was driving. And the lieutenant sat behind me and he explained what my assignment was, and he said that I should say such and such and such and such a thing. If I would not say all these things that he dictated to me, more or less, that I would pay for it with my life. And I said, "Well, perhaps I won't use the exactly -- exactly the same words," and he said, "Well, whatever. Just go on repeating it." And these were the words -- there was a loudspeaker on the car and there was a microphone in the car. So when I spoke, then the citizens, all around, could hear what I was saying. May I say straight away that I did not do this of my own free will. I want everybody here to understand that, that I did not do this of my own free will. And this is what the text was: "People of Samac, get out, surrender your weapons. I am" -- and then I gave my name and surname, and then I said, "See, nothing's happened to me, nothing will happen to you. Just take your weapons out and put them in front of your doors. If you are afraid of handing it in yourself, this is a Serb army and police, there is nothing to be afraid of, everything will be all right." And many did that, actually. I went to a certain street together with them, that way. Do you want me to go on with this description?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No. At this point, I'd like to interrupt you, and I apologise to you for this, but there is one detail that I omitted to obtain in respect of the episode where Simo Zaric appeared at the door and obtained the release of those men that you mentioned. The time that he did that, came to the cell and obtained the release of the men, what was the condition of the other prisoners who were in the cell with you and the men who were released? What did they look like? What sort of condition were they in?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Quite a few of them were already beaten up badly. I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts wasn't yet, because Crni said that they would be needing me and that's what they saved me. And I remember Cosevic [phoen] already had his ribs broken. At any rate, I said already that in that cell there were not any soldiers. All of them were civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What did they look like? That's what I'm interested in. What would Mr. Simo Zaric have seen when he walked in and saw these men? What sort of condition would they have been in?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that if he wanted to pay attention, he could have seen in a glance the situation which was pretty terrible, terrible. People were already bloody, beaten up. So he could have seen that the situation was pretty bad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Can I please get a clarification from you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Judge Singh, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Can I seek another clarification from you on that same point? A little earlier, you said Simo Zaric was there and the guard opened the door, and he said, "Let my guys out." And you later said, "It became clear to us who his guys were." Now, who said those words? Did the guard say those words or Simo Zaric said those words?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that I put it quite nicely. Perhaps the Honourable Judge did not quite understand what I was saying. The guard just opened the door. Mr. Zaric uttered those words. Are you satisfied with my answer, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SINGH
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Because the text says, "he said." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. And the other question is: Those guys who were let out after Simo Zaric said, "Let my guys out," how did they look?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None of them had been beaten.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: One other question on this topic. When Mr. Simo Zaric came to the cell and said, "Let my guys out," how was he dressed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just correct you. Mr. Zaric did not actually enter the cell.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not enter the cell. He stood in the corridor, and he had a camouflage uniform, also with a white band.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: From where he was standing in the corridor, would he have had a view into the cell?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a good view, because it's a two-metre-wide corridor and there are two cells. And it's not walls that are there or something else. These are typical cells, with bars on them, so he could see very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thanks. All right. Okay. Now, I interrupted you to get back to this description of events in the cell. Now can I ask you to go back and think about the time when you were taken out into the car and you had to speak into the microphone and inform the citizens to surrender themselves. Can you pick up your narrative?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I start answering now?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So this vehicle drove me through town for a while, until I got to near my house, and then from the direction of the entrance into Samac, I saw APCs. I'm sure about one. I'm not sure about the other one. Because my house is near my brother's house, and I really paid attention to this. And then I saw the barrel of this APC pointed at my brother's house. However, before that, another thing: I was taken out of the car by these two soldiers, and then these soldiers who were in the APC, or before the APC -- so this is a crossroads. This is where they got me out of the car and this is what they said, literally: "Here he is. We are handing him over to you now." And this man who handed me over, or those two men, these two soldiers who handed me over, were Fadil Topcagic, Cvikan Tesic, and some others. So I already got close to that APC. I saw that this APC had pointed its barrel against my brother's house. And then I heard this quite well. And then various things happened afterwards during this war, but this was the first time I saw Mr. Tadic, and I heard his words very well when he ordered this APC, that they should turn the barrel away, that upstairs there was a Serb who was living there and downstairs is a really good man. I was really pleased to hear that, because it was my brother, after all, that he was talking about. And then Fadil explained to me, in the briefest possible terms, what my task was, I mean what they meant when they said, "Now we are handing him over to you."

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who were you being handed over to?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I already knew everything by then. I had realised everything by then, who these military people were. These were members of the 4th Detachment and their task was to occupy Bosanski Samac. They handed me over to Fadil Topcagic and Cvikan, "Cviko," Tesic, and they issued all other orders to me, all the things I had to carry out against my own free will.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So the people into whose custody or control you were placed was Fadil Topcagic and the other man you have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Cvikan Tesic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was Miroslav Tadic apparently associated with those men? What I mean, was he working with them, together with them?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I shall describe to you the picture that I saw. If I manage to portray all of this for you, I think that it will confirm what actually happened. Behind this APC, a few metres away, in the same kind of uniform -- and now, I think, I think -- I cannot say this with certainty whether it was a camouflage uniform or a military uniform, but it was a uniform, at any rate, and also there was a white ribbon on the uniform, and he also had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Miroslav Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Okay. Now, you were handed into the custody of these men. What happened then?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then other things happened. They ordered me to go from one house to the other: Muslim, Croat. Well, at any rate, there was no need for them to enter the Serb houses, because they were already there. And they asked people to get their weapons out and to hand them over, if they had any, and this went on for, say, 20 minutes, half an hour, an hour. In all that fear, I had lost all sense of orientation in time, and I think that you will agree with me that this is only a normal thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you and ask you this: What were you doing during this particular time? What was your job or role?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My role was to walk in front of them, into all these Muslim and Croat houses, and to tell them to take weapons out, to hand them over. So I was some kind of an errand boy of theirs who was supposed to carry out their dirty work for them, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You said previously that you had to broadcast through the microphone reassuring messages to the Croats and Muslims. Did you have to do the same when you were going up to individual houses?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but of course I did not have a loudspeaker any longer, that kind of system. I would walk in and I would say, in a pretty loud voice - quite a loud voice, as a matter of fact - I would say, "Do not be afraid. Please hand in these weapons." They did not ask whether these weapons were legal or illegal. They took away everything, without any kind of certificate, nothing. If a person had a hunting gun, nothing. He just had to hand it over. He wouldn't get a certificate. If he had a legal pistol, he would have to hand it over. He would not get a certificate at all. He simply had to hand it over. If he had something illegally, then it was only understood that he had to hand this in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, during this particular process, when you were going from house to house, calling on people to surrender their weapons, what was Mr. Miroslav Tadic doing?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had lost sight of Mr. Tadic. They would always send me a few houses ahead in relation to the APC, so I cannot really confirm where Mr. Tadic was. I could not see him any more. And then perhaps a few minutes later, when I would already get away from the place where I was handed over from the police vehicle, he was there by the APC. And since I would always walk about 50 metres ahead with somebody from the 4th Detachment, I cannot really know what the gentleman was doing behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When you were going into houses, you were escorted by someone from the 4th Detachment; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. There was always somebody there. But I was invariably the first one ahead of everyone, and I had to repeat at every house, I had to repeat this thing time and again: "Don't be afraid. I'm Ibela." So every -- it's a small town. Everybody knew everybody. So I had to do part of their work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, if I could ask Mr. Salkic just one question. Concerning the broadcast in the car and the loudspeaker, and then also walking in front of the escort and saying, "Don't be afraid," et cetera, did you know or were you told what would happen to you if you refused to do either or both?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall answer that question. I have not been saying this, again, because I thought that what I said about the vehicle was sufficient. When I was speaking into the loudspeaker, they said, "Fine." If I did not do what they told me to do and if I did not say what I was supposed to say, that that would be the end of me. So that's why I thought that it wasn't necessary for me to emphasise that I was being threatened all the time and that my life was in jeopardy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you again.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What sort of weapon was Mr. Tadic -- I'll withdraw that question. Perhaps I should ask you this: Was Mr. Tadic armed when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I said that. Perhaps there was a mistake in the translation or something, but I did say that Mr. Tadic was in uniform, a marked one, and also that he was armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Now, did this walking around from house to house eventually cease?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Perhaps I'm going to describe this detail for you now as well. I came to the vicinity of the Fitozovic brothers' house. Oh, yes. Yes. Perhaps I haven't told you and the Court that, in the meantime, I also got a white armband.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I'd like you to explain to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is what happened then: A man in -- a gentleman in a camouflage uniform, with paint on his face, like this, he called me from Smail and Esad Fitozovic's house. They were people who were very well off. They had a shop with spare parts, car parts, and a big shop which was more or less like a mini supermarket. I remember these words very well. I remember this is what he said to me: "Come here, brother. You're supposed to do something for us." I was dead from fear. Although they put this armband on my arm, perhaps he did not think that I was one of them, but he did think I was one of them. And then he said, "Take this suitcase." And then he took a box of Marlborough cigarettes out and gave me two packs and said that I could keep them and said that I should take this to the police station and that over there I should emphasise that this is for Lugar. That is the first time I heard the name Lugar. This was a big, heavy bag. Of course, I didn't dare look inside. So I carried this, and it was not easy to carry that and the box of cigarettes. It's not that it was that heavy but it was bulky. In the meantime, a vehicle came by, the same vehicle that took me out of the SUP. They stopped by me and they asked, "What's that?" And I explained what it was. And then they said to me that I should go on foot, that I should walk in the middle of the street with my hands up, and that I should walk that way all the way to the police station. And that's exactly what I did. So I came to the police station and that's where they started beating me straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Could I just stop you there, please? First of all, who put the armband on your arm? And were you ever -- was an explanation ever given --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Fadil Topcagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did he explain why, why he was doing that, what the reason was?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, so that there was no misunderstanding. But everything was clear to me straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What I mean is, did he say anything to you at the time that put -- he gave you the white armband to wear?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he said something along the lines of the following, that I was theirs, but it was all a very quick conversation, a quick exchange, and as we knew each other fairly well, there was some other words, but I can't quite remember them all now. But this was a sort of form of security for me, that at that particular moment I was not a Muslim, I was not a Croat either, I was a Serb, because all the Serbs were marked in that same way, with that armband.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What I want to know is, did he have anything in mind for you at that particular moment by giving you the white armband? Did he want you to start fighting or do something specific? What caused him to put on -- put the armband on you at that point, at that time? For what reason? As far as you can tell.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably, maybe something along those lines as well, but I understood it -- and actually he said that to me, he repeated the words he uttered earlier on. He said, "Well, you have chosen the right side." So he thought that it was enough for me to -- for him to put that white armband on me for me to be the 4th Detachment. I can't remember all the details, but that was the gist of it. I was afraid and lots of -- many years have passed by since then, and I'm doing my best to tell the truth and say something that I'm 100 per cent certain of. Perhaps it would not always coincide with the statement I gave. Some other things might have been mentioned there. But I don't want to say anything that I'm not 100 per cent certain about now. So can it just stay there? Can we leave it there, that those were the words he actually spoke?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, Mr. Salkic, were you still wearing the white armband when you arrived at the police station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you mean the first time or when I returned on this other occasion?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: I'm talking about what we just mentioned now, when you arrived at the police station and you were beaten immediately you got in.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And they even swore at me, they cursed my balija, Muslim, Ustasha mother, because, "Look at him," they said, "he's marked himself with this band." I hadn't actually done so, but they beat me and said that I had declared myself, and, yes, they beat me because of that, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you still have the possessions that Lugar had given you?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had handed them over before that to the guys, the soldiers that came by in the car. They took the car and those things, and I said that I was afraid because Lugar, he -- that the man had threatened me, he had paint on his face and it was ugly to see. And he threatened me and said that I was -- must be sure to take that to the police station and not to give it to anybody else. They confiscated it from me, but they said that I should go on foot to the MUP with my hands raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to get this sequence clear in my head. Fadil Topcagic puts the white armband on you, you start walking back to the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. They put the white armband on me quite a bit before, the first time I was handed over to them. That's when they put the armband on. And everything I did before I went into there, I already had the armband on me, and I came to the police station with the armband on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When you were going into the houses and asking -- and telling the Croats and Muslims that everything was okay, did you have the white armband on?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you have it on when you first met the man you later knew to be Lugar?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You say that you started walking back to the MUP. Why did you do that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had taken the things that that man, who was later to introduce himself as Lugar to me -- he was wearing a camouflage uniform, he had the armband, he had paint on his face, and I froze when I saw him, not to speak of anything else. He ordered this. He ordered me to do this because he saw the white armband, he said, "Ej, bre, brate," in the way that would you address a fellow Serb. So that was a certainty. I'm sure that that was what he thought. Otherwise ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You took the bag from him and you started going back to the MUP; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you have your arms in a surrender position at that stage?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I was still carrying the things. I couldn't have carried the things otherwise. My hands were freed only when those two men took the things away from me and loaded them up. I said that this was for some man called Lugar and that this was to be handed in at the police station, and they said, "That's our business. We will do that." And then they ordered me to raise my hands up because I couldn't have raised my hands carrying the bags and the boxes, could I?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand the sequence now. Is that when you walked back with your hands raised to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did they tell you to keep your hands raised?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those two, the two soldiers who took me from the MUP to hand me over to the others, they also confiscated those things. No, they didn't confiscate. They helped me. They took them off my hands. So I had to go down one street onto the main road which led to the MUP with my arms raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How far did you have to go before you got to the MUP? A kilometre, half a kilometre, 200 yards -- 200 metres? How far?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 800 metres to a kilometre at the most. Between 800 metres and one kilometre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Why didn't you make a run for it, try and escape, get away from this?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I have already explained that very well, but let me answer your question. Samac had already been surrounded so there was nowhere you could flee to. Everything was closed off. Where could you go to? All you could do was to try and escape, and that would be tantamount to death. So I had no choice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Have you got any idea why you were chosen to encourage people to surrender their weapons?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you analyse the situation a bit, if you have time and analyse the offence, it's very simple to arrive at an answer. The four people were already from the 4th Detachment, so they weren't for it. But I moved around town a lot, saw people a lot, I had this little shop of mine. I played handball for the town team. Lots of people knew me. So probably, at that particular moment, I was useful to them, the best choice perhaps, compared to the others that were there. Had they got Tihic or Izetbegovic, well, they were politicians, they would have chosen them before me, but as they weren't there, then I was most suited to their purposes, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you said that you returned to the SUP and that you were beaten. Who beat you when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I arrived, in the corridor inside, they kicked me with their legs, beat me with their hands. We couldn't wait to get into the cell and be locked up because then not everybody could take aim at us. So somebody kicked me, somebody swore and cursed my balija mother or my Ustasha mother or Muslim mother or whatever. So in all that fear, I couldn't wait to get into the cell to get away from the corridor and away from that open space.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I take it you succeeded in getting into the cell?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How long did you remain in the SUP or the MUP?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stayed in the MUP -- let me see, that night, I spent that night in the MUP, and then the next day, in the morning, I was transferred to the TO building, the Territorial Defence building, which is opposite the MUP building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. di Fazio, I wonder whether, Mr. Salkic, you could just clarify. Mr. di Fazio had asked you who beat you when you arrived at the MUP, and you answered that "they" beat you and then described in part the beatings. Could you clarify who the "they" were, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I wasn't thinking of the people shut up like me. I meant the police, the police who were there, wearing either police uniforms or camouflage uniforms, who happened to be there. They beat me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: And do you know who those people in those uniforms were? Did you know their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I knew some of them. I didn't know others. But later on, I was to get to know many of them: Lugar, Laki, Beli, Avram. Now, which of them was there at that particular moment, I don't know. I know that Stevan was there among them, and then, begging your pardon, he kicked me in my butt, and told the others to "Shut that balija up there." So there were these people from Serbia, then there were some other locals, but one of them, as I say, was Stevan Todorovic, whom I knew before the war well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do I take it -- has Your Honour finished?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do I take it from your answer that it was a combination of locals and people apparently from Serbia who participated in beating you in -- upon your arrival back in the SUP, after having walked around the town?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That too. That wasn't quite clear to us yet. Judging by the dialect, we were able to conclude very easily that they weren't from our area, because we all spoke in a specific way, whereas they spoke Ekavian, so I noticed straight away that they weren't from our region, from our parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You were taken to the TO the next day. Can you recall whether it was the morning or the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in the morning, not very early, about 8.00, between 8.00 and 10.00. I can't really judge what the time was. I lost all sense of time. But it was in the morning, let's say between 8.00 and 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What happened at the TO?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They put us up there. We went through the TO yard. And then they found a room for us there on the left-hand side. The things that were in the room were thrown out so that the room was empty, left empty, just the floor and the walls, and they put us in there for a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So you were amongst the first guests at the TO, I gather from the fact that there was material in the room that had to be thrown out; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. There was some pieces of timber, wood, some kinds of bars or rods. It was a room used -- as I said before, they took away the weapons, so there were just some bits and pieces, rods and bars, left there. But this came in handy to them later on during our stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How many -- I'll withdraw that question. What sort of numbers were now imprisoned in the TO?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Before we got there -- let me just go back to one detail, if I may be allowed to, if -- while we were in the MUP, we spent such terrible time there, because 20 or 30 of us were crammed into these two cells, which were approximately two by a metre and a half. We weren't allowed to go to the toilet. We had no water, no food. At no time did they give us water, food, or allow us to go to the toilet while we were in the MUP, so that -- you can imagine -- and I'm sorry to have to say this, but people urinated where we were, and it was a very small space. So this, as far as the width and space were concerned, was like a hotel compared to the space we were in before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So do I take it that the numbers in the TO, initially at least, when you were taken there, were in the range of 20 to 30 people, 20 to 30 men?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And was it the case that all the people who you were with in the MUP were all transferred over to the TO?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown F1, F5 and F50 from Exhibit P14A. Perhaps when the usher has those photographs ready, he could present F5 on the ELMO first.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, what does that -- do you recognise that room?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's it. That's the room. But let me state that when we were brought there, there were no bars. The bars weren't there, all this red bit up there. It was just glass and a metal door, but none of these bars or grids. This is looking out into the yard from the room inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. For the purposes of the transcript, if Your Honours please, the witness is looking at photograph F1 of Exhibit P14A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now look at F5, please. That door on the left, do you recognise that door?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's the same thing. That's the entrance. But the bars weren't there either; just the metal door, no bars.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now F50, please. Can you quickly show the Chamber, show Their Honours, where the room that we've just seen in the previous two photographs is. Use the baton. Just point it out.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere here. I think that's the door, the first one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I've finished with the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How long did you remain in that TO building altogether?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the TO building. I was there from that week, the morning of that week, when they brought us from the MUP, up until the Sunday evening, so that seven-day period. The following week, we left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: For where?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They then took us to Brcko. So I spent eight days in the TO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just a thing for clarification. In our language, "Sunday" and "the week" is the same word, so when he says "the morning of that week," he means the morning of Sunday. In the transcript, it says "that week," but I believe that the witness was testifying that the morning of Sunday when he was transferred to the TO building. So if my colleague can clarify that. This is page 68, 2 and 3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sure Mr. di Fazio will clarify the days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Is this the position: You were taken to the TO on the Sunday first?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When did you leave for Brcko?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A week later, which means the following Sunday. Eight days, from Sunday to Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want to ask you some questions about that period of eight days. Were more prisoners brought into the TO?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What was their ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was the process of bringing in prisoners a continuous one or did it happen on one or two occasions? In other words, did they come in a bunch or did they come in dribs and drabs over the next week?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One would come one day, the next day two or three, the next day four or five. So not all at once. They would come at certain intervals and different numbers, so that by -- so that the number increased quite considerably.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who was bringing them in?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police, the guards. I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did any of them appear to be soldiers?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were they locals?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the Monday that you were in the TO. On that day, were you taken anywhere?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They hadn't taken me anywhere that day yet, because there was an overture, if I can put it that way, to that conversation, or, to be more specific, they did that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I do apologise, Mr. Salkic. I think I understand what you mean. Did you see Lugar on that Monday morning?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw several of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Well, now, that's what I'd like you to tell us about. Can you tell us under what circumstances you had the pleasure of Mr. Lugar's company on Monday morning?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was like this: He turned up -- we were getting to know these Serbs from Serbia and their special forces, as they were to introduce themselves later on. Lugar came and he gave us his name and surname, although we had already become acquainted with him. Avram, Laki, Beli, the others. And among them was a local Serb whose nickname was Cera. I don't know his surname, but they all referred to him as Cera. Then they called us out by name and surname, one by one: Omer Nalic, Hasan Bicic, Muhamed Bicic. I was among them; there was Roma, and some others, about five or six of us. And the purpose of us being taken out was, of course, well, beating. I can't even describe that. We were all bloody, broken, black and blue, hardly able to stand on our own two feet. They had to pull some of us up because we had fallen down and were kneeling. But let me continue with what happened to me. That same man, Lugar, gave me a piece of paper and a pencil, and all bloody and beaten up that I was, he forced me to write a statement for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. I, unfortunately, do want you to recount the beating before you were given the piece of paper and forced to write the statement. First of all, where did the beating occur?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I have a little water, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: There's a jug just there.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is how it was: They took me out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: I was about to say, it's 1.00. Yes. Can we have a break?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I'm sorry, I didn't realise the time, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. The court clock is 1.00, so we go for the lunch break and resume the proceedings at 1530 hours. --- Luncheon recess taken at 1.01 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. di Fazio, you're continuing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. If Your Honours please, a matter arises from the issue that I raised briefly with you earlier today, namely the statement or alleged statement of this witness that was taken in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In Brcko?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In Bosanski Samac, yes. I very briefly spoke to Mr. Zecevic just now and I understand that he is in two minds as to whether or not he will use the document; a matter for him. However, the Prosecution, having now come into the possession of this document by Mr. Zecevic handing it to us, I can tell the Chamber that we are very particularly interested in the document and regard it as very important that we put the matters -- put the statement to this witness. And that exercise that I spoke about earlier is assumed even more importance in my mind now. And it's crucial, from our point of view, that we conduct that exercise before the completion of my examination-in-chief of Mr. Salkic. So when that can be attended to, I'm not entirely sure. It's being translated as we speak. I've had a rough translation put to me -- given to me by the interpreters. We are doing whatever we can to get it translated, officially translated, as quickly as possible. And I will do my level best to make sure that the investigator can speak to the witness about that document with -- armed with the proper official translation as soon as possible. If everything went well, that -- ideally that would be this evening. But if it doesn't go well, and if the translation is not there and if we can't get the investigator to Mr. Salkic tonight, then at some stage it will have to be done, and tomorrow it's crucial, from the Prosecution's point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We can hold onto that. You can go ahead and deal with that, but that shouldn't hold the proceedings, because if you can't get the document ready before you finish examination-in-chief, we can stand this witness down.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And proceed with another witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And then when you're ready at the right juncture, then we bring him back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I just wanted to raise that possibility. I'm hoping that this will come to nothing and I'll be able to come back to court tomorrow armed with fresh instructions and the matter will proceed smoothly, God willing. That would be an ideal outcome, and I'll do what I can to bring that about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: In case that doesn't happen, let's not hold the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. May I just now produce another two documents to the Court? Copies have been given to my learned friends. They are purely and simply the dates of the orthodox and non-orthodox Easter in 1992. They are obtained from a web site, the U.S. Naval Observatory, I believe. Copies have been given to my learned friends. It's just to establish and fix the dates of Easter, 1992. Can I provide the Chamber with copies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It consists of two documents. I don't know if Your Honours have marking pens, but for the sake of simplicity, I can quickly guide you to the relevant entries. On one document you have -- it's entitled "The Date of Easter," simply "The date of Easter."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. As you go -- as you describe this one, maybe we can have the numbers, if there's no objection to the -- from the Defence. Yes. I don't think so. Can we have the numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document with "The Date of Easter" will be Prosecution Exhibit P30. The other document, "The Date of Orthodox Easter," will be Prosecution Exhibit 32.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. And on P30, if Your Honours please, if you turn over the page, you'll see three columns. In the first column, towards the end, it establishes April 19, 1992 as the - I'm not quite sure of the terminology - as the non-Orthodox Easter of that year. And on P31 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Is it P31 or P32?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Can I make a correction, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: "The Date of Easter" is P31 and "The Date of Orthodox Easter" is P32.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So if you look at P32, "The Date of Orthodox Easter," it's on about the fourth page of the document dealing with the Gregorian calendar, and that establishes, about two-thirds of the way down the first column, that the 26th of April, 1992, was Easter in the Orthodox church. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Salkic, before the break, you were about to tell us of an encounter that you had with Lugar on the Monday morning, the Monday that you had been -- after you had been initially transferred to the TO, and you got as far as telling us that you were taken outside and started to -- instructed to write a statement. And I was interested in what happened in the period of time just before you actually sat down to write that statement. You said that a number of men were taken out. Were they also instructed to write statements?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They told all of us, all of us who had already been taken out, to do that. But let me describe the event that took place before we started writing the statements. Can I do that? May I be allowed to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Please do. That's exactly what I want you to do. Tell us in detail what happened.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They called out the names: Ibela, Hasan, Beca, Mesa, Roma, Omer Nalic, all these names. About five or six people were taken out, and there were some outside already. And this was our official introduction to Lugar, Laki, Beli, Tralja, Avram, and all the rest of them who I was to meet subsequently. And the beating started. How, I'm going to try and describe them to you in detail now. First of all, it was enough to give your name. They would take what they found, what they had to hand - the chair, the leg of a chair or some other object or implement - because there was a garage nearby where there was a small truck, an old, small truck, which was full of discarded objects: chairs, metal objects. And they started beating us, and that went on for at least, at least, a half hour. We were all broken, all bloody. It was really astounding that any of us had remained alive. So at that time, with all that going on and all the fear that experienced, Lugar said to one of the others, "Give them the papers and the pencils." And then they cursed our balija, Muslim, Ustasha mothers, whatever they felt like. And we took up the papers. We didn't know what statements we were expected to write. And I remember one of us asked, "What do you want us to write?" And Lugar kicked him with his foot and said, "Well, write down, you balija motherfuckers, who gave you the weapons, where you were taken to," where this, where that. So some of us succeeded in writing down the statement in the state they were in. I think that, after a great deal of trouble, I too managed to write some sort of statement down, but what the statement was like -- well, I can describe that to you again, because I was to encounter that statement later on. The statement was in fact all bloody, covered in blood. I wrote down what did happen and what didn't happen, because, quite frankly, my life was at stake, and not only my life but the life of all the others, all the other people who were with me. So I wrote down everything I could think of. I managed to write down the statement. I'm not sure whether I signed it. I think I did. But I don't know how they were able to read it from all the blood that was dropping onto the paper from this injury that I had in this place here. There was a hole in my head and my hand was all bloody, and I was writing as the blood was pouring out of my hand and out of my head. And I'm really interested in how the person reading the statement could have managed to read it with all the blood that was on the paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If the witness could be shown F50. Thanks. Sorry, photograph number 50 from Exhibit P14A.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you do your best and try and point out where the area, at least, where you and the other men were beaten?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here you have it. That's the yard. This is the door we came out of. This is the yard, and this is the garage where that little truck was, with the various objects, metal and wooden, inside. So we wrote all this down on the ground. We had nothing to rest the paper on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Right. So beating and writing of statement occurred in the courtyard? Answer so that it's on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You may or may not be able to recall, but were those gates open or closed that you can see in the photograph, the corrugated iron gates?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well; the gates were closed. They were very rarely open.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Usher, I've done with the photo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What about sound? During the course of the beating, could -- did the victims, yourself included, scream, yell, make a noise?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were terrible screams, and while they were beating us and while those screams could be heard, the others who were in the room, they had to start singing, because during the few days that we were incarcerated, they had taught us to sing their - I can say this quite frankly - Chetnik songs, because I doubt very much that they were Serb songs, folk songs. They were purely Chetnik songs, the ones that they told us to sing. So let me -- my answer to your question is yes, yes, there were screams, because it was terrible pain that the people were suffering, and in addition to that, we had to listen to the songs, the Chetnik songs that they made us sing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. After the statement -- after you'd written whatever you did write on the statement, were you taken somewhere?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They brought us back inside. They had to carry some people inside because they were in such bad shape, but they took us back to the room. And after some time, they called me out to the SUP or MUP again where they showed me the bloody statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Just stop there. Were you escorted across the road to the SUP?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The guard took me there. And as I was going into the hallway, I saw beatings going -- there were beatings, but that is -- when I was brought upstairs to the office, they didn't beat me any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. What did you see in this office that you were taken to?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw some people that I knew very well in that office. I knew them very well by then. There was Simo Bozic, Milos Savic, Vlado Sarkanovic, Topolovac and Mr. Zaric, who was in the hallway at the MUP at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Pause there. Bozic, Saric, Sarkanovic and Topolovac, what ethnic background were they?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are Serbs. Let me say it wasn't Saric, it was Savic, Milos Savic was the man's name, not Saric. They were Serbs, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. My apologies, it was my mispronunciation, thank you. What sort of work did Bozic, Simo Bozic, and Milo Savic do prior to this date? What was their job?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All four of them already worked at -- in the police force, but the two of them, Sarkanovic and Topolovac, had already retired, whereas the other two were still working.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were they local --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the police. No, just one moment, I have one more error to put right. Mr. Bozic was a judge already. He was in fact a magistrate, a misdemeanour judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I see. What was your condition when you first entered the room?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was covered in blood because we didn't have where to wash. The blood had dried. It was all over our clothing. Our health was poor. We were -- briefly speaking, we were in a very sorry state.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned Simo Zaric was in the -- I think you said in the corridor or the hallway. Was that close to the office that you eventually ended up in?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the gentleman came in for a brief moment. I think we said hello. He glanced at me and went out, followed by Sarkanovic and Topolovac, and Bozic, Mr. Bozic, and Milos Savic remained inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did he say anything when he came in? I'm now referring to Mr. Simo Zaric.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think he talked to the Judges or the investigators, or I don't know what to call them, because there were interrogations that were taking place. I can't now remember, but they said that they ought to finish with me, something along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, you've told us about the statement that you had given to Lugar. What had you done with the statement after it was completed, when you were still back in the courtyard writing it out? What had you done with it, the piece of paper, the actual piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I handed it to Lugar, and this is what happened next: That same statement was placed on the table in front of me, all bloody, when I was at Mr. Simo Bozic's and Mr. Savic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they asked me what it was that I had written. They weren't satisfied with what I had written, actually, but I could give them nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can I just interrupt you there? Let's go through it slowly, okay? When you got into the room, when you first entered the room, was the statement visible?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How long after you entered the room did Simo Zaric come into the room?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't remember exactly, because I was terrified. You must understand, the Prosecution and the Defence and the Trial Chamber, because thank goodness none of you have ever had to experience anything like it, so it's very difficult to remember all the details, but I'm doing my best Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts to tell you what I remembered and how I remembered it. I think several minutes went by, one, two, three, five. It wouldn't be honest of me if I were to say -- tell you to the minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. I appreciate that time has passed, and I ask no more than you do your best, but if you can recall, do tell us. Is it now your position that one or two or three or five minutes passed before Simo Zaric entered the room?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, yes. It didn't last long. It was very brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: At the time he entered the room, was the statement visible?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I saw her later -- I saw it later, I'm sorry, I saw it later, when Mr. Bozic produced it. Mr. Bozic showed it to me while he questioned me. Maybe it was in front of him for quite some time before that, but I couldn't see it because he was on the other side, but when he turned it round and placed it in front of me, then I saw that it was indeed my bloody statement, covered in blood.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So Mr. Bozic was obviously aware of your statement because he produced it; is that correct? Just answer yes or no. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Savic presumably was aware of your statement because he was there as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was anyone else aware of the existence of that statement? Anyone else who came into the room?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that conversation of ours, that same statement could have been seen by Mr. Zaric, if he wanted to, of course he could have seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did he ever comment on it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What did he say?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said the following words to me: "You have enumerated some names here. You mentioned the names of people who have gone across the Sava River, and you haven't included the ones who are in town." And I said that I had been there for several days, that I didn't know who had left, who had escaped and who was still in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Now, how long were you in the interview for?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean that particular time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. How long --

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. How long were you in that room, speaking to these men?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not long. It went on for another couple of minutes. Milos - no, I'm sorry - Simo Bozic. After that, Mr. Zaric was no longer there. He went off somewhere. I don't know where. I continued talking with the other two men; that is to say, they conducted the interview with me, and they said that I should say -- tell them things, and I kept saying that I didn't know who did this, who did that. And they said, "Well, if you don't want to do it of your own accord, we'll force you." And then they took me back. Once again, I was escorted through the corridor. Nobody beat me on the first floor, but when I went downstairs to the ground floor, there was always someone there, some policemen from Serbia, and we had to pass them through the hallway. And then they took me back to the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can I just ask you to pause there. Before we leave the interview altogether, you have told the Chamber that one statement was taken from you, for want of a better expression, by Lugar. During the course of this second interview over the road in the MUP, was a statement actually taken from you and produced, put on paper?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they put it on paper, I don't know about that. I don't remember. I did not write it myself. I did not write any statement by myself. It was an interrogation, really.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Were you asked to sign anything in the MUP on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know what you signed?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Believe me, now I can't say. I can't say either yes or no. Perhaps I did sign it, perhaps I didn't, but I'm not sure, so I would not want to give an inaccurate answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Salkic. Were you taken back to the TO?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I described my journey to there briefly. From the offices where I was interrogated, and when I was not beaten, when I went downstairs, as I was going downstairs, they started kicking me and hitting me with rifle butts. I managed to glance briefly to the right, where the cell was where I had been. There were other people there, and I could not recognise them that quickly. They took me across the street and they took me to that room where the rest of them were at the TO.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now I want to ask you about conditions in the TO for that week, thereabouts, before you were transferred to Brcko. You've mentioned briefly the singing of Chetnik songs. Can you tell the Chamber how often that would occur? And bear in mind that I'm now talking about that first week in the TO.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As any one of their soldiers passed by us, they would beat us. The singing was compulsory. These Serbs from Serbia came and ordered us to sing out loud all the time, to sing those songs, and the people at the MUP and at the municipality could hear that very well, very well. There are gentlemen here who worked at the municipality, and they could hear that singing very well. People did not have water, they were beaten up, they did not have adequate food. And people would start falling because they had to remain standing for so long, and we had to lift them up, because the others would say, "If you don't remain standing, we'll kill you." So then we had to lift them all the time, because Lugar had actually said that he could kill people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Sead Mujkanovic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What was his job in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a policeman, a policeman at the MUP in Bosanski Samac.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: His ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He's a Muslim. As I said, he worked at the police station. I can tell you, unfortunately, a bad thing that happened to him there in that room. Lugar walked in, and simply, in cold blood, he asked him who he was, directly. So he came there with the intention of looking for Sead Mujkanovic. He walked in. Sead was sitting there, and he simply took an army rifle which has a sight here on the top. I don't know how to explain this to you, all the details. But he shoved it into his mouth. He turned it around and he pulled it out. And I'm not sure now whether two or three of his teeth simply fell out this way. He also kicked him. He kicked him with his army boot and he fell, and he cursed his balija, Ustasha, whatever, mother. And then he started kicking all of us around. And then he simply said, "Get up." And he was cursing our balija mothers, Ustasha mothers, and then singing again. All of this happened within those two or three days at the TO: singing, people passing out, and then we had to lift them. And that's how it went on until we went to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I will need to get more details about what happened in the TO. Before I do that, can I ask you to clarify one thing: Did the incident with Sead Mujkanovic occur in the courtyard or did it occur in the room in which you were imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened in the room. It happened in the room. I can describe that room. We saw it here in that picture. When you enter through the door, on the left side was where Mr. Sead Mujkanovic was sitting, and that's the room where he pulled his teeth out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you about a gentleman named Omer Nalic. Do you know him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was he imprisoned with you in the TO in this first week before you were taken to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: His ethnic background, please?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You've mentioned a gentleman named Cera. Did Cera ever have any dealings with Omer Nalic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think so. But I can describe this particular occurrence for you, what happened to Omer Nalic, because it wasn't only Omer Nalic who was involved in all of this. I was there, and the Bicic brothers, Didic [phoen]. It was always a certain group. They always took out four or five or perhaps six men. They would start beating us. Lugar was also there, Laki, Beli. I think that this was the first moment when I saw Cera. I mean, I had seen him with them before that, but this was the first time I saw him take some kind of action. He called Omer and he moved him a metre away from us, and he said that if he wanted to buy his life, that he should give 5.000 Deutschemarks. And I heard this very well when he said, Omer said, "Cera, I haven't got this. What do you mean? I haven't got any money here in the camp." And he kept his hands this way, and he was explaining all this to him. And up here, up here, he stuck a knife through his arm and he swore at his balija mother. There was something else that really surprised him, because he also swore at his managerial mother, because Omer was a manager at the power supply company. They he took him away, and then Omer told us that he went to -- around town. He went to his wife, he went to see his friends, and that he gave him a certain amount of money. So I cannot really confirm this, but in essence, he bought his own life. In Omer's absence, they beat us some more. They took us back and then the usual thing: singing, singing these Chetnik songs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. What's a managerial mother? I don't follow you.

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know, Omer was a manager, a manager in a company, so it was because of the position that he held. He was cursing his mother, so then his managerial mother, like he was a manager, and he had cursed his balija mother before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the wound that Nalic suffered, how did that progress? Did you see -- have an opportunity to see the wound over the ensuing days?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, because Omer and I spent quite a bit of time in camp together, so we could all see this non-stop. It was a wound up here, a cut across the arm. It looked very, very bad because it got infected. We didn't have any kind of medical help there. There wasn't anyone who could dress his wound or something, or any one of us who were there, so it was a horrible, horrible thing to look at, this wound. It was bleeding for a long time. It got infected. That kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, for the purposes of the transcript, the witness has identified his left forearm as the site of the wound he has described.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was this an isolated episode of extortion or did it occur on other occasions in that first week that you were in the TO?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. This happened several times, quite often. They asked me and the Bicic brothers, and they often came to beat people and to ask for car keys, because these two guys were quite well off. They had shops and cars. And they beat them quite often, and they took the two of them -- no, not the two of them, one of them, to collect some money and also to buy his own life. I think it was Lugar and Beli who did this. And now, whether they managed to do that or not, at that moment, everybody was afraid to say either yes or no, and I was pretty sure that it was that way. Once, after that, Lugar came and hugged the two of them, which surprised us, and he said, "Oh, boy, I have no idea what you have done to these Serbs. You are such good men. Why are you being treated that way? They even want to have you killed, and you are good men. What do these local Serbs have against you, hold against you?" That's the comment I heard myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You have said that you were a victim of extortion yourself. Can you describe to the Chamber what happened in your case?
