utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. They came there to ask me for money, but I really didn't have any, not at home, not with me. There was just a bit, 700, 800 Deutschemarks. I managed to give them that, and they asked for more, but I really didn't have any more, so they beat me up. They probably heard from the others, the Serbs from Serbia, I mean -- I want to underline that with the exception of Cera, all this was done by the Serbs from Serbia, not by the local Serbs, with the exception of Cera, and Cera probably being aware of my situation, he probably said, "What he gave is enough, coming from him." So they had beaten me up, but then they didn't mistreat me after that. There was some local currency, just a little bit, but that was basically worthless.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where did you eat in the first week that you were in the TO?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I would have to point this out. While we were at the police, at the MUP, we absolutely had nothing to eat. Only when we were transferred to the TO, one morning a truck came and I think that a certain person called Lazo, nicknamed Trojan, came, and he put us into this truck and he took us to the restaurant of the Utva company, and that's where we had breakfast.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How often did you eat there? Was it just this one occasion or were there other occasions?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We went there perhaps during the first two or three days, so we went twice or three times altogether. So we had the opportunity of seeing what was going on. And even some of these people who were not attached to the military or to the police, who worked there at the kitchen, we asked them what was going on, things like that. So it was only two or three days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: On those occasions that you went to the Utva factory, did you see any of the defendants or the accused?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I saw Mr. Milan Simic, only once. I looked at him. In a way, he was -- in a way, I was happy. I thought perhaps I'd hear something from him. However, I had the feeling that he was embarrassed because of all of this. He put his head down and walked away, went to a restaurant, to a dining hall. I worked in this company so I knew the layout well. This was a dining hall for business luncheons. This was my first contact. This was the first time I saw Mr. Milan Simic. We did not have any contact. It's not that we talked or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where were you prisoners taken to eat in Utva? Where in Utva?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The restaurant that was actually a cafeteria where all the workers at that company had their meals.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And where is the dining hall for the business luncheons? Is that the same place or is it some other location?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there, there, there. There is a single entrance, and then when you go through that door, on one side is the restaurant for business luncheons, where business partners of this company came, and to the right-hand side, or rather, straight ahead was the kitchen where you would actually get the food, and then the tables were on the other side, the restaurant, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: After you sighted Milan Simic, did you -- were you able to see him throughout the time that you were eating there, or did he just disappear from sight?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. He had left. I explained this. Perhaps it was difficult to translate it. I had the feeling that when he saw us all soaked in blood, beaten up, that he was ashamed, that he was embarrassed, and that he went to that restaurant, because all of these people practically were people that he knew very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman nicknamed Dikan?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I met him in camp. I had not known him before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What was his ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: About how old was he?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he was a pretty small man. My estimate is that he was perhaps between 45 and 50, perhaps a bit more, perhaps a bit less. I don't know. I know who the gentleman is. We were there together for a few days. But I cannot really tell his age. Say between 45 and 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Was he a robust, strong man?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was a small man. Perhaps he weighed about 45 kilos. He was also quite short, perhaps 160 centimetres in height, a very small man, slight. However, they beat him often. They said allegedly that he was a Zenga, that his sons were Zengas, and that his sons were there in Croatia, in the Croatian National Guard Corps. They often took him out to beat him. He was such a small man, such a skinny man, I don't know what they had to beat except his bones, but they beat him a lot. And then ultimately he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Can you explain what a Zenga is?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll try. Zenga is an abbreviation, you know, of the Croat army, and it is actually the Croatian National Guard Corps, Zbor Narodne Garde, so in our language, this is an abbreviation, ZNG. I don't know whether I succeeded in doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Is it used as an insulting term or is it just simply a term of description?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was just a term, the Croatian National Guard Corps. But for them, it was something hostile. It implied that it was the enemy. It was like the SDA. The SDA was just a party, but for them it was the enemy. Can you understand that? For them it was just an enemy army, although this was an army from a neighbouring state.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Before I ask you to describe the fate of Dikan, I'd just like to ask you some questions about the guards and those carrying out the beatings. You have said that those carrying out the beatings in that week were men from Serbia and that Cera was the only local who participated in beatings. Did you have guards who were there on a more or less permanent basis or working in shifts?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they worked in shifts. I don't know how often they changed, but out of the locals, I think -- well, I guess that many, many people before me talked about this, or other people who will come in will tell you about this. It hardly ever happened that Mr. Todorovic would not come to see us. He's a local man. But then also the guards were coming in, and these men from Serbia proper were forcing them to beat us. These local people, they probably wouldn't want to beat us, but they made them beat us. I don't know why. And then they got to like it too, and then the locals started beating us regularly too. Not all of them. I always underline that: not all of them, but some of them. For example, this Jajcinoivc person, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've said that you were transferred eventually to Brcko. When in relation to that occurrence did the murder - or sorry - the death of Dikan occur: days before, on the same day? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dikan's murder occurred on the Orthodox Easter. It was a Sunday. It happened in the afternoon hours. Screams were heard. There was lots of commotion. They came in drunk, because they were probably celebrating, which would have been a normal thing under normal circumstances, that they were celebrating their Easter. Lugar came with some other men. He started shooting through the door. He broke the door open. The first person who was next to the door was the late Dikan. When the door was opened, with a rod or stick or something - I don't know - I was - you could put it this way - clinically dead from fear. Now I can even laugh and say this. He hit this Dikan, and Dikan fell. And then he took this Ustasha, as he had put it. He said, "Give me this Ustasha. Pull him out." And then they pulled him out. And then something was heard, like one gunshot or several gunshots. I don't know. I went numb. And then one of them ended up in Dikan's head. Soon after that, Lugar and these guys left and the guards came and asked, or rather, ordered them -- somebody else to carry Dikan away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just a couple of questions from your last answer. Did he use the rod or stick to hit Dikan?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was an object.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, whatever it was that he had in his hands, did he use that to beat Dikan?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes. Dikan was a small man. One blow in the head was sufficient. Dikan fell. I think he was dead by then. I don't think he even had to shoot him in the head.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And who was ordered to carry him out?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. The guards came. I was beside myself. I think it was Safet Srna, or Sead Srna. I don't know. I'll get confused. And also, Muhamed and Hasan were there too, and they said they couldn't -- I don't know. I don't know. I cannot remember well. This was great fear. You've got to understand this. It's ugly for me to make this kind of comparison, but imagine if somebody were to spill somebody's brains here in front of all of you in this courtroom. I think that it would take months and years for you to recover from that, let alone remember things. I was lucky. Immediately after this event, a guard came and took me to the SUP. If you ask me more about this, I'm going to tell you about this event that had to do with me, and I talked about it in my statement too. Actually, you can proceed with your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just bear with me for a moment, please, Mr. Salkic. Where were you taken to in the SUP?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A guard came and said that I had to go up and have a talk. I went upstairs and -- perhaps I would have taken advantage to thank him. Mr. Simo Zaric came by in the corridor, who took me off to an office and said that I should sit there while he saw to some business he had - because he had some major problems that I already knew about - but that Lugar and him could go back and do something worse, so that it was better for me to stay on in his office. And of course, that's what I did. And then he came by once or twice to ask whether I had any problems. I said no. Then he came to fetch me after some time had gone by and told me that I was going and that the others were going too, to some other place, a safer place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Where did that turn out to be?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't know anything yet. They got us onto a truck. There was a police and military escort. And as it was night, it was difficult to differentiate and see where we were going. But as I knew those parts, I glanced out, although I didn't dare look, but I was sure they were taking us in the direction of Grebnice, Slatina, Obudovac, Loncari, and Brcko, ultimately. So that as the canvas on the truck had a hole in it, I was able to peek through and I was able to get my bearings, because I knew those parts very well. We ended up in the JNA barracks in Brcko, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, we'll get on to the transfer to Brcko in due course, but I want to ask you something about interviews. In that week that you were in the TO, were you ever shown any lists of people?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they kept bringing out some plans and lists, who needed to liquidate whom, which Muslims, which Serbs, and I assumed that that was only a pretext for them to be able to beat us more.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: This liquidation of Serbs, were you ever given any list or confronted with any list or accused of any plans to liquidate Serbs?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, there weren't any plans, but they did show some lists, but not lists for killings. For example, that I was supposed to kill Topcagic, the other one was supposed to kill Simo Zaric, the other some other person, that kind of thing. I didn't dare say this publicly, but of course I thought that was all nonsense.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes. Who confronted you with these allegations?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, it was Savic and Bozic. They asked me some questions. And on one occasion, Mr. Zaric came in and asked me whether I really -- whether I was really supposed to kill Fadil, and I said that nothing of the sort would ever enter my head, especially not to kill somebody for no reason at all. And he sort of laughed. So I too realised that it was a sort of, if I can dare say, joke or provocation or some such thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When did this allegation from Mr. Zaric -- when was it made?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. It was twice that I met Mr. Zaric -- I met Mr. Zaric twice, and I'm not quite sure when this was. It was always a difficult moment. I think those allegations could have been the Sunday that I was to go back, maybe up in the office, when they were going to transfer us to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You met the allegation with -- with words to the effect that nothing of the sort would ever enter your head, especially not killing someone for any reason at all. Do I take it from that answer that you took the allegation seriously?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could have been taken seriously, because you never knew. They were saying things that were not logical. They wanted you to own up to something you didn't do. I'm not speaking about Mr. Zaric in this connection. I'm just speaking in general of what happened during those events. Now, if they said something like this, you would be in a dilemma. You can't know whether he meant it seriously or not. And I always -- well, we knew each other for so long, for so many years back, then I think -- and I think he knew that I could never kill Fadil or anybody else. I think he knew me well enough. So it's difficult for me to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about what Mr. Zaric thought. I'm not asking you whether he took it seriously or whether he thought it was a joke. I'm not asking you about that. I'm asking what you thought, your reaction -- just hear me out. I'm interested in your reaction. Now, you've told the Court that nothing of the sort would enter your head, especially not to kill anybody -- somebody for no reason at all. Now, my question is: Given that answer that you made, did you, in your own head, in your own mind, take the allegation seriously at the time that it was made? In other words, did you think you had to give a serious answer to it?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at all events, yes, because the question was raised and I answered it. I answered it seriously. I said seriously that I would never do anything like that, nor would it enter into my mind to do so, but subconsciously, in my subconscious, I thought it might have been different.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. So the -- you've mentioned that you were transferred to Brcko. How was that done? Train, truck, airplane?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in a truck. They loaded us up, and we had an escort, as I said earlier on. The police were following us, and in front of us, there were one or two vehicles, jeeps, and I saw them when I got off. By the sound of the motor, I knew that -- the engine, I knew that there was something in front, and I saw that they were jeeps. And that's how we were transferred to the barracks in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What happened as you were taken off the trucks?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were ordered to come out one by one. It was in front of this building, seven, eight, ten metres away. There were armed soldiers there, and we got off one by one. Somebody would hit us with their leg, kick us, or with their hand, but nothing terrible. We went inside, and we were searched. We had to spread our legs, hold our hands up behind our necks. Anybody that had anything, money, wallets, jewellery, everything was confiscated. And then we went to the right, into a corridor, where they tied our hands, and put us into two rooms, two adjoining rooms, next to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who was transferred from Bosanski Samac? Was it the entire group that was in the TO or were some left behind?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the TO, not everybody came. Some people stayed. I can remember some of their names. A couple of them stayed. At first, I didn't know that they had stayed behind, because I was in the SUP prior to the departure when we -- before we got onto the truck, but when we got there, they told me that several people had stayed behind for some sort of exchange. There was Izet Izetbegovic and there was a man called Ivo Matic. They, unfortunately, killed him. There was Luka, who was the policeman on duty. He was killed too. There was a man named Baja, they called him Baja, from Domaljevac. He was exchanged, but he died shortly afterwards from the results -- consequences of everything. So about five people stayed behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stayed in Brcko up until the 31st of April or 1st of May. I'm not quite sure of the date, but I do know that it was the day when we heard in the morning, early, two very strong explosions, and we were to hear afterwards, from what the guards said, that two bridges had in fact been blown up in Brcko. One was the railway bridge and the other the other one. And they transferred us to Bijeljina that morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I want to -- I don't want to leave Brcko so soon. Can you tell the Chamber if you or any of the other prisoners were interrogated in the time that you were at Brcko?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who conducted interrogations there?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally was not interrogated. I made no statements in Brcko, but others did, and everybody said that it was Mr. Zaric who conducted the interrogation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you actually lay eyes on him whilst you were at Brcko, see him, see him around the place?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I saw him on several occasions. The first time was that evening when they brought us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So you say that he accompanied you to Brcko? Is that your position, from Bosanski Samac to Brcko?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't go with us, but probably in some other vehicle, yes. And I saw him a couple of other times, in the morning. So we came in the evening to Brcko, and the next day, in the morning, he came with a captain who was there. He was some sort of a superior. And when they saw the state we were in, Zaric asked him to put a bit of order into all that, and to ensure that we had medical assistance. So I saw him two or three times during that period when the interrogations took place of my colleagues from detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did you, in fact -- I'll withdraw that. Did any of the prisoners receive any medical assistance whilst at Brcko?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: What sort of assistance was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: [redacted]. Him and Dragan Lukac were the worst -- in the worst condition, and they were the ones who badly needed assistance. And then they did some other little things for others, bandaged up a wound or something like that. It wasn't much, but they did a good job, given the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How could you see -- if you weren't interrogated, how could you see Mr. Zaric about the place?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The room I was incarcerated in and the others were next to each other. There were two rooms next to each other, so that the person coming into the building, whenever anybody saw him, they would say, "Here comes Simo. We are going to be up for an exchange." And he would always come from the front side, and he would pass by our windows in order to enter the building. And he would go in -- he would go to the left-hand side because that's where the offices were. So I was able to see him very, very well, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: How long would he remain there?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He would stay from, say, 8.00 or 9.00 in the morning - I'm not quite sure what time - until 12.00 or 1.00. I don't know exactly. I didn't pay that much attention. But it went by very slowly. Five, six, seven or eight of them, in those two or three days, succeeded in giving their statements. I did not make a statement there. However, may I just add that when Mr. Zaric left, and that captain who was with him, I don't know what his name was, all hell broke loose again after they had left. And when I say "hell," I mean the beatings, the blows, but I should also like to emphasise that you did not dare make a sound, even if they were breaking your bones, and you were not allowed to make a sound. We knew why; because Brcko was a free town. War had still not come to Brcko, and this was a sort of Yugoslav People's Army, and I thought that this was our chance, that we would be saved, and that we would live. However, they did do a service for us; they transferred us from Samac to the barracks where the conditions were better, but not much better, not much better. So that means that they did intend -- that had they wanted to help us really, they could have opened the truck doors and said, "You're free to go." But they left us. We went from one bad situation to a worse situation, and our sufferings were greater and greater.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: During the week that you were in Brcko, were any of your fellow prisoners taken away, taken away from Brcko?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. One day Mr. Zaric came by. I saw him. Now, whether they went with him, I don't know. I saw Fadil Topcagic and some others. The guard came and called their names out: Omer Nalic, Hadzialijagic, and Mr. Tihic. Their names were called out. I don't know if there was anybody else with them. I can't remember now. And quite simply, they took them away. We didn't know where.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Did they return?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did return. And that surprised us, because they came wearing new clothing, they were shaved, they were washed. The only thing they couldn't do was to remove the bruises under their eyes. And later on, I learnt that they were given sunglasses. So that was what happened. And they told us that they had been taken to make statements. And we joked about this, made fun of them and said that they were media personalities now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: In the time that you were at Brcko, was Simo Zaric the only defendant that you saw?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On one occasion I saw Mr. Milan Simic as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at that period of time, in those couple of days. I can't remember exactly what day it was, one day or another day, but I do know that he was there with Fadil and Djuheric. I think that Mr. Simo was already inside. Whether they had come there together or they met up there, I don't know. I can't say. But they didn't come together. Simo was already inside. The others were giving statements as their names were called out, and then they came later on and were there in front.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would Your Honours just bear with me for a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I just want to ask you some more questions about this sighting of Milan Simic. Where were you when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in that room where we were incarcerated. I could see him very, very well, because he was in front of me, some eight, ten, to twelve metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You were looking through a window?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were windows with bars on them, so that you could see through the windows. You could see who was coming up to the building, leaving the building, and quite a lot of area around the building was visible. But we would often have a dilemma. We saw people walking up and down beyond the fence. And it looked as if freedom was at hand, and so when you saw someone like that coming up, like I saw Fadil in a group, and Mr. Simic, and that man Djuheric, you always have some hope that that's the end of it, that they had come to fetch us to take us home. We always had this hope. And I sort of liked to see them. But as I say, I could see him very, very well, to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Who was this man Djuheric?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djuheric.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise for my mispronunciation, but who was he?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a local Muslim from Bosanski Samac who was a member of the 4th Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: When you saw Milan Simic, he was apparently in company with this man and Topcagic?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and they were all wearing uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: About how long did you see him for? Was it just a glance, or did he stop and talk to others so you were able to look at him for a long time? What sort of time period are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It didn't last long. A couple of minutes. Because then they left. When they got out of the car, they passed along a path. They stopped there for a while. Fadil explained something and motioned with his hands, describing where we were, whether to Simic or to Djuheric. And then they moved along the path towards the gate and the other section of the barracks. Where they went off, I don't know. I didn't see them after that. But it lasted one and a half to two minutes perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Mr. di Fazio, I wonder whether the witness could tell us what were the uniforms that Mr. Simic and the other gentleman was wearing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: You heard Her Honour's question. Can you describe what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. They were wearing camouflage army uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WILLIAMS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: All right. Now, I think in an earlier answer you said that you were taken to Bijeljina and that followed shortly after some explosions that took place in Brcko. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just tell us briefly how you were transferred from Brcko to Bijeljina. What means was used?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let me start in this order: In the morning, we saw that something was amiss. The soldiers were coming in and out of the barracks, and we saw that something was wrong, that something was happening in Brcko. And they ordered us to come out one by one. They put a white cloth around our eyes and took us off to the buses. But not everyone. I can't remember now whether it was the captain or somebody else. The two or three people who had had their eyes tied said that they told them that they would be able to take them off later. We got into the buses. Nobody beat us while we were getting to the buses. Then the soldiers stood around and asked, "What are we going to do with these?"

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you. Do I take it, then, that the transfer to Bijeljina was done by bus?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I just want to ask you about some of the other men you've mentioned. Lukac, Tihic, [redacted], were they with you on this bus to Bijeljina or not?

utterances.speaker: IBRAHIM SALKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were still with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: It's 5.00, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Would this be an appropriate time to break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. We will rise and continue tomorrow at 0930 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 2nd day of November 2001, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.00 p.m.,
